19-
20---  ## Behavioral Equivaleence
21-
22---  In an earlier chapter, we investigated the correctness of a very simple
23---  program transformation: the `optimize0plus` function. The programming
24---  language we were considering was the first version of the language of
25---  arithmetic expressions -- with no variables -- so in that setting it
26---  was very easy to define what it means for a program transformation to
27---  be correct: it should always yield a program that evaluates to the same
28---  number as the original.
29-
30---  To talk about the correctness of program transformations for the full
31---  Imp language -- in particular, assignment -- we need to consider the
32---  role of mutable state and develop a more sophisticated notion of
33---  correctness, which we'll call *behavioral equivalence*.
34-
35---  For example:
36-
37---  - `X + 2` is behaviorally equivalent to `1 + X + 1`
38---  - `X - X` is behaviorally equivalent to `0`
39---  - `(X - 1) + 1` is *not* behaviorally equivalent to `X`
40-
41---  ### Definitions
42-
43---  For `aexp`s and `bexp`s with variables, the definition we want is
44---  clear: Two `aexp`s or `bexp`s are "behaviorally equivalent" if they
45---  evaluate to the same result in every state.
46-
47-def Aexp.Equiv (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : Prop :=
48-  ∀ (st : State),
49-    a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st
50-
51-theorem Aexp.equiv_def {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} :
52-    a₁.Equiv a₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st := by rfl
53-
54-def Bexp.Equiv (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : Prop :=
55-  ∀ (st : State),
56-    b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st
57-
58-theorem Bexp.equiv_def {b₁ b₂ : Bexp} :
59-    b₁.Equiv b₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st := by rfl
60-
61---  Here are some simple examples of equivalences of arithmetic and boolean
62---  expressions.
63-
64-example : Aexp.Equiv
65-    (aexp { X - X })
66-    (aexp { 0 }) := by
67-  rw [Aexp.equiv_def]
68-  intro st
69-  simp
70-
71-example : Bexp.Equiv
72-    (bexp { X - X = 0 })
73-    (bexp { true }) := by
74-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def]
75-  intro st
76-  simp
77-
78---  For commands, the situation is a little more subtle. We can't simply
79---  say "two commands are behaviorally equivalent if they evaluate to the
80---  same ending state whenever they are started in the same initial state,"
81---  because some commands, when run in some starting states, don't
82---  terminate in any final state at all!
83-
84---  What we need instead is this: two commands are behaviorally equivalent
85---  if, for any given starting state, they either (1) both diverge or else
86---  (2) both terminate in the same final state. A compact way to express
87---  this is "if the first one terminates in a particular state then so does
88---  the second, and vice versa."
89-
90-def Com.Equiv (c₁ c₂ : Com) : Prop :=
91-    ∀ {st st' : State},
92-      (st =[ ~c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ ~c₂ ]=> st')
93-
94-theorem Com.equiv_def {c₁ c₂ : Com} : c₁.Equiv c₂ ↔
95-    ∀ {st st' : State}, (st =[ ~c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ ~c₂ ]=> st') := by rfl
96-

98-

101---  For examples of command equivalence, let's start by looking at a
102---  trivial equivalence involving `skip`.
103-
104-theorem skip_left {c : Com} : (imp { skip; ~c }).Equiv c := by
105-  rw [equiv_def]
106-  intro st st''
107-  constructor
108-  · intro h
109-    inversion h with
110-    | seq st' h1 h2 =>
111-      inversion h1
112-      exact h2
113-  · intro h
114-    exact EvalR.seq EvalR.skip h

119---  equivalent program.
120-
121-theorem skip_right {c : Com} : (imp { ~c; skip }).Equiv c := by
122-  rw [equiv_def]
123-  intro st st''
124-  constructor
125-  · intro h
126-    inversion h with
127-    | seq st' h1 h2 =>
128-      inversion h2
129-      exact h1
130-  · intro h
131-    exact EvalR.seq h EvalR.skip

133---  Similarly, here is a simple equivalence that optimises `if` commands.
134-
135-theorem if_true_simple {c₁ c₂ : Com} : (imp {if (true) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}).Equiv c₁ := by
136-  rw [equiv_def]
137-  intro st st'
138-  constructor
139-  · intro h
140-    inversion h with
141-    | ifTrue hb hc => exact hc
142-    | ifFalse hb hc => simp at hb
143-  · intro h
144-    apply EvalR.ifTrue _ h
145-    simp
146-
147---  Of course, no programmer would write a conditional whose condition is
148---  literally `true`. (At least, no human programmer -- compilers and macro
149---  preprocessors do this sort of thing internally all the time!) But they
150---  might write one whose condition is *equivalent* to true:
151-
152---  Note to developers (Sati @satiscugcat):
153---      The to_verso script seems to use `\[\]` blocks, but these seem to
154---      cause problems with the tilde. Currently skipping them and just
155---      using backticks.
156-
157---  *Theorem*: If `b` is equivalent to `true`, then
158---  `if (~b) {~c₁}
159---  else {~c₂}` is equivalent to `c₁`. *Proof*:
160-
161---  - (`->`) We must show, for all `st` and `st'`, that if
162---    `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` then
163---    `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`.
164-
165---    Proceed by cases on the rules that could possibly have been used to
166---    show `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`, namely
167---    `Com.EvalR.ifTrue` and `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`.
168-
169---    - Suppose the final rule in the derivation of
170---      `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` was
171---      `Com.EvalR.ifTrue`. We then have, by the premises of
172---      `Com.EvalR.ifTrue`, that `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`. This is exactly what
173---      we set out to prove.
174-
175---    - On the other hand, suppose the final rule in the derivation of
176---      `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` was
177---      `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`. We then know that `b.eval st = false` and
178---      `st =[ c₂ ]=> st'`.
179-
180---      Recall that `b` is equivalent to `true`, i.e., forall `st`,
181---      `b.eval st = (bexp {true}).eval st`. In particular, this means that
182---      `b.eval st = true`, since `(bexp {true}).eval st = true`. But this
183---      is a contradiction, since `Com.EvalR.ifFalse` requires that
184---      `b.eval st = false`. Thus, the final rule could not have been
185---      `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`.
186-
187---  - (`<-`) We must show, for all `st` and `st'`, that if
188---    `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'` then
189---    `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`.
190-
191---    Since `b` is equivalent to `true`, we know that `b.eval st` =
192---    `(bexp {true}).eval st = true` = `true`. Together with the assumption
193---    that `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`, we can apply `Com.EvalR.ifTrue` to derive
194---    `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`.
195-
196---  Here is the formal version of this proof:
197-
198-theorem if_true {b : Bexp} {c₁ c₂ : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
199-    (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}).Equiv c₁ := by
200-  rw [equiv_def]
201-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
202-  intro st st'
203-  constructor
204-  · intro h
205-    inversion h with
206-    | ifTrue hb' hc =>
207-      exact hc
208-    | ifFalse hb' hc =>
209-      rw [hb] at hb'
210-      simp at hb'
211-  · intro h
212-    apply EvalR.ifTrue _ h
213-    rw [hb]
214-    simp

264---  For `while` loops, we can give a similar pair of theorems. A loop whose
265---  guard is equivalent to `false` is equivalent to `skip`, while a loop
266---  whose guard is equivalent to `true` is equivalent to
267---  `while (true) {skip;} end` (or any other non-terminating program).
268-
269---  The first of these facts is easy.
270-
271-theorem while_false_equiv {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {false})) :
272-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
273-    (imp {skip}) := by
274-  rw [equiv_def]
275-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
276-  intro st st''
277-  constructor
278-  · intro h
279-    inversion h with
280-    | whileFalse => exact EvalR.skip
281-    | whileTrue st' hb' hc hloop =>
282-      simp [hb] at hb'
283-  · intro h
284-    inversion h
285-    apply EvalR.whileFalse
286-    simp [hb]

288---  ### Exercise (2 stars): while_false_informal (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐
289-
290---  Write an informal proof of `while_false_equiv`.
291-
292---  To prove the second fact, we need an auxiliary lemma stating that
293---  `while` loops whose guards are equivalent to `true` never terminate.
294-
295---  *Lemma*: If `b` is equivalent to `true`, then it cannot be the case
296---  that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`.
297-
298---  *Proof*: Suppose that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. We show, by
299---  induction on a derivation of `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`, that this
300---  assumption leads to a contradiction. The only two cases to consider are
301---  `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` and `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`; the others are
302---  contradictory.
303-
304---  - Suppose `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` is proved using rule
305---    `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`. Then by assumption `b.eval st = false`. But
306---    this contradicts the assumption that `b` is equivalent to `true`.
307-
308---  - Suppose `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` is proved using rule
309---    `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`. We must have:
310-
311---    1. `b.eval st = true`, and
312-
313---    2. there is some `st₀` such that `st =[ c ] => st₀` and
314---       `st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`.
315-
316---    3. Also, we are given an induction hypothesis saying that
317---       `st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` leads to a contradiction,
318-
319---    We obtain a contradiction by 2 and 3.
320-
321-theorem while_true_nonterm {b : Bexp} {c : Com} {st st' : State} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
322-    ¬ st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st' := by
323-  intro contra
324-  generalize heq : (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) = com at contra
325-  induction contra with
326-  | @whileFalse b' s0 c0 hb' =>
327-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
328-    subst hbeq
329-    rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
330-    simp [hb] at hb'
331-  | @whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b' c0 hb' hc' hwhile ih1 ih2 =>
332-    exact ih2 heq
333-  | skip | asgn | seq | ifTrue | ifFalse =>
334-    contradiction -- heq says that different commands are equal
335-

342---  Prove the following theorem. *Hint*: You'll want to use

344-
345-theorem while_true {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
346-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
347-    (imp {while (true) {skip}}) := by
348-  rw [equiv_def]
349-  intro st st'
350-  constructor
351-  · intro h
352-    exfalso
353-    exact while_true_nonterm hb h

355-    exfalso
356-    apply while_true_nonterm _ h

358-    intro
359-    rfl

361---  A more interesting fact about `while` commands is that any number of
362---  copies of the body can be "unrolled" without changing meaning.
363-
364---  Loop unrolling is an important transformation in any real compiler, so
365---  its correctness is of more than just academic interest!
366-
367-theorem loop_unrolling {b : Bexp} {c : Com} :
368-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
369-    (imp {
370-      if (~b) {~c} else {skip};
371-      while (~b) {~c}
372-    }) := by
373-  rw [equiv_def]
374-  intro st st'
375-  constructor
376-  · intro h
377-    inversion h with
378-    | whileFalse hb =>
379-      apply EvalR.seq (st' := st)
380-      · exact EvalR.ifFalse hb EvalR.skip
381-      · exact EvalR.whileFalse hb
382-    | whileTrue stmid hb hc hloop =>
383-      apply EvalR.seq _ hloop
384-      exact EvalR.ifTrue hb hc
385-  · intro h
386-    inversion h with
387-    | seq stmid h1 h2 =>
388-      inversion h1 with
389-      | ifTrue hb hc =>
390-        exact EvalR.whileTrue hb hc h2
391-      | ifFalse hb hc =>
392-        inversion hc
393-        exact h2

448---  ## Properties of Behavior Equivalence
449-
450---  We next consider some fundamental properties of program equivalence.
451-
452---  ### Behavioral Equivalence is an Equivalence
453-
454---  First, let's verify that the equivalences on `Aexp`s, `Bexp`s, and
455---  `Com`s really are *equivalences* -- ie, that they are reflexive,
456---  symmetric, and transitive. These proofs are all easy.
457-
458-end Com
459-
460-theorem Aexp.equiv_refl (a : Aexp) : a.Equiv a := by
461-  rw [equiv_def]
462-  intro st
463-  rfl
464-
465-theorem Aexp.equiv_symm {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} (h : a₁.Equiv a₂) : a₂.Equiv a₁ := by
466-  rw [equiv_def] at h ⊢
467-  intro st
468-  rw [h]
469-

471-    a₁.Equiv a₃ := by
472-  rw [equiv_def] at h₁ h₂ ⊢
473-  intro st
474-  rw [h₁, h₂]
475-

479-  rfl

508---  ### Behavioral Equivalence is a Congruence
509-
510---  Less obviously, behavioral equivalence is also a *congruence*. That is,
511---  the equivalence of two subprograms implies the equivalence of the
512---  larger programs in which they are embedded:
513-
514---  aequiv a a' ------------------------- cequiv (x := a) (x := a')
515-
516---  cequiv c1 c1' cequiv c2 c2' -------------------------- cequiv (c1;c2)
517---  (c1';c2')
518-
519---  ... and so on for the other forms of commands.
520-
521---  (Note that we are using the inference rule notation here not as part of
522---  an inductive definition, but simply to write down some valid
523---  implications in a readable format. We prove these implications below.)
524-
525---  We will see a concrete example of why these congruence properties are
526---  important in the following section (in the proof of
527---  `fold_constants_com_sound`), but the main idea is that they allow us to
528---  replace a small part of a large program with an equivalent small part
529---  and know that the whole large programs are equivalent *without* doing
530---  an explicit proof about the parts that didn't change -- i.e., the
531---  "proof burden" of a small change to a large program is proportional to
532---  the size of the change, not the program!
533-
534-theorem Com.congruence.asgn {x : Ident} {a a' : Aexp} (ha : a.Equiv a') :
535-    (imp {x := ~a}).Equiv
536-    (imp {x := ~a'}) := by
537-  rw [equiv_def]
538-  intro st st'
539-  constructor <;>
540-  · intro h
541-    inversion h with
542-    | asgn n h =>
543-      subst h
544-      apply Com.EvalR.asgn
545-      rw [Aexp.equiv_def] at ha
546-      rw [ha]
547-
548---  The congruence property for loops is a little more interesting, since
549---  it requires induction.
550-
551---  *Theorem*: Equivalence is a congruence for `while` -- that is, if `b`
552---  is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to `c'`, then
553---  `while (~b) {~c}` is equivalent to `while (~b') {~c'}`.
554-
555---  *Proof*: Suppose `b` is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to
556---  `c'`. We must show, for every `st` and `st'`, that
557---  `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` iff `st = while (~b') {~c'}
558---  ]=> st'`.
559---  We consider the two directions separately.
560-
561---  - (`->`) We show that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` implies
562---    `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, by induction on a derivation of
563---    `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. The only nontrivial cases are when
564---    the final rule in the derivation is `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` or
565---    `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`.
566-
567---    - `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`: In this case, the form of the rule gives us
568---      `beval st b = false` and `st = st'`. But then, since `b` and `b'`
569---      are equivalent, we have `beval st b' =false`, and
570---      `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` applies, giving us
571---      `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, as required.
572-
573---    - `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`: The form of the rule now gives us
574---      `beval st b = true`, with `st =[ c ]=> st'0` and
575---      `st'0 =[ while {~b} {~c} ]=> st'` for some state `st'0`, with the
576---      induction hypothesis `st'0 =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`.
577-
578---      Since `c` and `c'` are equivalent, we know that `st =[ c']=> st'0`.
579---      And since `b` and `b'` are equivalent, we have
580---      `beval st b' = true`. Now `Com.EvalR.whileTrue` applies, giving us
581---      `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, as required.
582-
583---  - (`<-`) Similar.

93---  not consciously recognize them as "theorems." But properties that seem
94---  intuitively obvious can sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also

55+-- In an earlier chapter, we began applying the mathematical tools developed
56+-- in the first part of the course to studying the theory of a small
57+-- programming language, Imp.
58+
59+-- - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with an
60+--   *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that specifies the
61+--   *operational semantics* of programs.
62+
63+--   The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key features of
64+--   full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the fundamental
65+--   notion of mutable state and some common control structures.
66+
67+-- - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the sense
68+--   that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather than of
69+--   particular programs in the language. These included:
70+
71+--   - determinism of evaluation
72+
73+--   - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions (e.g.,
74+--     functional and relational definitions of arithmetic expression evaluation)
75+
76+--   - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
77+
78+--   - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of useful
79+--     program transformations
80+
81+--   - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the Equiv chapter).
82+
83+-- If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of tools
84+-- for defining and discussing programming languages and language features
85+-- that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work with, applied
86+-- to a set of key properties. All of these properties are things that
87+-- language designers, compiler writers, and users might care about knowing.
88+-- Indeed, many of them are so fundamental to our understanding of the
89+-- programming languages we deal with that we might not consciously recognize
90+-- them as "theorems." But properties that seem intuitively obvious can
91+-- sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also subtly wrong!).
92+
93+-- In another volume of this series (*Type Systems*), we expand upon the theme
94+-- of metatheoretic properties of whole languages when we discuss *types* and
95+-- *type soundness*. In this chapter, though, we turn to a different set of
96+-- issues.
97+
98+-- Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work through some
99+-- simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
100+-- definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
101+-- particular specifications of their behavior.
102+
103+-- We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic* -- often
104+-- shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of the syntactic
105+-- constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be used
106+-- to reason compositionally about the correctness of programs involving this
107+-- construct.
108+
109+-- Hoare Logic originated in the 1960s, and it continues to be the subject of
110+-- intensive research right up to the present day. It lies at the core of a
111+-- multitude of tools that are being used in academia and industry to specify
112+-- and verify real software systems.
113+
114+-- Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of writing down
115+-- *specifications* of programs, and a *structured proof technique* for
116+-- proving that programs are correct with respect to such specifications --
117+-- where by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs directly mirrors
118+-- the structure of the programs that they are about.
119+

122+--     what we've done and of this chapter, but it never mentioned Hoare logic!
123+--     The text above seems like a better intro.

128+--

131+--           - abstract syntax trees
132+--           - evaluation functions (for [aexp]s and [bexp]s)
133+--           - evaluation relation (for commands)
134+--
135+--      - Proved some _metatheoretic_ properties
136+--          - determinism of evaluation
137+--          - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the
138+--            definitions (e.g., functional and relational definitions of
139+--            arithmetic expression evaluation)
140+--          - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
141+--          - meaning-preservation of some program transformations
142+--          - behavioral equivalence of programs ([Equiv])
143+--
144+--      We've dealt with a few sorts of properties of Imp programs:
145+--        - Termination
146+--        - Nontermination
147+--        - Equivalence
148+--
149+--      Topic:

151+--          correctness_ of programs in Imp
152+--

155+--        - a _compositional_ proof technique for program correctness
156+--
157+--      Plan:

159+--        - proof rules
160+--        - loop invariants
161+--        - decorated programs
162+--        - examples`

167+-- formally, a predicate of `State`s.

225---  ### Notations for Assertions
226-
227---  This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two
228---  reasons: (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to
229---  begin with `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that
230---  we ever use to look up variables in assertions (we will almost never
231---  need to talk about two different memory states at the same time). For
232---  discussing examples informally, we'll adopt some simplifying
233---  conventions: we'll drop the initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just
234---  `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus, instead of writing
235-
236---    fun st => st[X] = m
237-
238---  we'll write just
239-
240---    {{ X = m }}.
241-
242---  Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
243---  assertion. We'll see more examples below.
244-
245---  This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout
246---  the Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like
247---  `X`, `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`,
248---  `y`, `m`, and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is
249---  why, when translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with
250---  `st[X]` but leave `m` alone.

218+
219+-- This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two reasons:
220+-- (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to begin with
221+-- `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that we ever use to
222+-- look up variables in assertions (we will almost never need to talk about
223+-- two different memory states at the same time). For discussing examples
224+-- informally, we'll adopt some simplifying conventions: we'll drop the
225+-- initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus,
226+-- instead of writing
227+
228+--   fun st => st[X] = m
229+
230+-- we'll write just
231+
232+--   {{ X = m }}.
233+
234+-- Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
235+-- assertion. We'll see more examples below.
236+
237+-- This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout the
238+-- Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like `X`,
239+-- `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`, `y`, `m`,
240+-- and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is why, when
241+-- translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with `st[X]` but leave
242+-- `m` alone.

257+--     `HIDE: SAZ 2024:

261+--     [(fun st => a st + b st)], neither of which is stable under
262+--     simplification.  For example:
263+--

265+--         (fun st => (X:Aexp) st + (Y:Aexp) st) st +
266+--         (fun st => (Z:Aexp) st) st)]

272+-- The convention described above can be implemented with a little syntax
273+-- magic, using coercions and a custom grammar, much as we did with the
274+-- `imp { … }` notation in Imp. This new notation automatically lifts `Aexp`s,
275+-- numbers, and `Prop`s into `Assertion`s when they appear between the
276+-- `{{ _ }}` brackets, or when Lean knows that the type of an expression is
277+-- `Assertion`.
278+
279+-- There is no need to understand the details of how these notations work.

292+--     that these functions should always be unfolded during simplification

296+--     Ans: If [a : aexp] then in the assertion_scope [(X →ₜ a st; st)] and

298+--     thanks to the coercion [Aexp_of_aexp].`
299+--
300+--     Claude suggested `@[simp]`-tagged characterizing lemmas next to the

315+--     Inside that scope, variables, arithmetic and boolean expressions,

633+-- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
634+
635+-- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
636+-- command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in this
637+-- book, is
638+
639+--   {{P}} c {{Q}}
640+
641+-- meaning:
642+
643+-- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
644+-- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
645+-- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
646+
647+-- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
648+-- *postcondition*.
649+
650+-- For example,
651+
652+-- - The Hoare triple
653+
654+--   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
655+
656+-- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
657+-- a state in which `X = 1`.
658+
659+-- - On the other hand,
660+
661+--   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
662+
663+-- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
664+-- `{{X = m}} X :=
665+-- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
666+-- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
667+-- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
668+
669+-- _Quiz:_
670+
671+-- Paraphrase the following in English.
672+
673+--   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
674+
675+--   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
676+
677+--   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
678+
679+--   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
680+
681+--   5) ∀ m,
682+--        {{X = m}}
683+--        c
684+--        {{Y = real_fact m}}
685+
686+--   6) ∀ m,
687+--        {{X = m}}
688+--        c
689+--        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
690+
691+-- _Quiz:_
692+
693+-- Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the claimed relation
694+-- between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
695+
696+--   {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
697+
698+-- (A) Yes
699+
700+-- (B) No
701+
702+-- _Quiz:_
703+
704+-- What about this one?
705+
706+--   {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
707+
708+-- (A) Yes
709+
710+-- (B) No
711+
712+-- _Quiz:_
713+
714+-- What about this one?
715+
716+--   {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
717+
718+-- (A) Yes
719+
720+-- (B) No
721+
722+-- _Quiz:_
723+
724+-- What about this one?
725+
726+--   {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
727+
728+-- (A) Yes
729+
730+-- (B) No
731+
732+-- _Quiz:_
733+
734+-- What about this one?
735+
736+--   {{True}} skip {{False}}
737+
738+-- (A) Yes
739+
740+-- (B) No
741+
742+-- _Quiz:_
743+
744+-- What about this one?
745+
746+--   {{False}} skip {{True}}
747+
748+-- (A) Yes
749+
750+-- (B) No
751+
752+-- _Quiz:_
753+
754+-- What about this one?
755+
756+--   {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
757+
758+-- (A) Yes
759+
760+-- (B) No
761+
762+-- _Quiz:_
763+
764+-- This one?
765+
766+--   {{X = 0}}
767+--     while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end
768+--   {{X = 1}}
769+
770+-- (A) Yes
771+
772+-- (B) No
773+
774+-- _Quiz:_
775+
776+-- This one?
777+
778+--   {{X = 1}}
779+--     while X ≠ 0 do X := X + 1 end
780+--   {{X = 100}}
781+
782+-- (A) Yes
783+
784+-- (B) No
785+
786+-- ### Exercise (1 star): valid_triples ⭐
787+
788+-- Which of the following Hoare triples are *valid* -- i.e., the claimed
789+-- relation between `P`, `c`, and `Q` is true?
790+
791+--   1) {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
792+
793+--   2) {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
794+
795+--   3) {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
796+
797+--   4) {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
798+
799+--   5) {{True}} skip {{False}}
800+
801+--   6) {{False}} skip {{True}}
802+
803+--   7) {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
804+
805+--   8) {{X = 0}}
806+--       while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end
807+--     {{X = 1}}
808+
809+--   9) {{X = 1}}
810+--       while X ≠ 0 do X := X + 1 end
811+--     {{X = 100}}
812+
813+-- All are valid except the 5th.

838+-- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
839+-- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
840+-- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
841+-- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.

938---  ## Proof Rules
939-
940---  The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for
941---  proving the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the
942---  structure of a program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of
943---  the program itself. To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce
944---  a rule for reasoning about each of the different syntactic forms of
945---  commands in Imp -- one for assignment, one for sequencing, one for
946---  conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple of "structural" rules for gluing
947---  things together. We will then be able to prove programs correct using
948---  these proof rules, without ever unfolding the definition of
949---  `ValidHoareTriple`.
950-
951---  ### Skip
952-
953---  Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
954-
955---    --------------------  (hoare_skip)
956---    {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
920+-- ## Proof Rules
921+
922+-- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
923+-- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
924+-- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
925+-- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
926+-- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
927+-- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
928+-- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
929+-- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
930+-- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
931+
932+-- ### Skip
933+
934+-- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
935+
936+--   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
937+--   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
957938 
958939 theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
959940     {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
962943   inversion h
963944   exact hpre
964945 
965---  ### Sequencing
966-
967---  If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q`
968---  holds, and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R`
969---  holds, then doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P`
970---  holds to one where `R` holds:
971-
972---     {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
973---     {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
974---    ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
975---    {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
946+-- ### Sequencing
947+
948+-- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
949+-- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
950+-- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
951+-- where `R` holds:
952+
953+--    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
954+--    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
955+--   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
956+--   {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
976957 
977958 theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
978959     (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
984965     rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
985966     exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
986967

990---  the natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end
991---  of the program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions
992---  backwards through commands until we reach the beginning.

968+-- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
969+-- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
970+-- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
971+-- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
972+-- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
973+-- through commands until we reach the beginning.
974+
975+-- ### Assignment
976+
977+-- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
978+-- rules. Here's how it works.
979+
980+-- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
981+
982+--   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
983+
984+-- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
985+-- could the precondition be?
986+
987+-- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
988+-- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
989+
990+--   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
991+
992+-- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
993+-- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
994+-- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
995+-- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
996+-- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
997+
998+-- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
999+
1000+--   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1001+
1002+-- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
1003+-- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
1004+
1005+--   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1006+
1007+-- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
1008+-- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
1009+-- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
1010+-- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
1011+-- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
1012+-- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
1013+-- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
1014+
1015+-- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
1016+-- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
1017+-- expression `a`:
1018+
1019+--   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1020+
1021+-- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
1022+-- replaced by `a`.
1023+
1024+-- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
1025+-- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
1026+
1027+-- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
1028+
1029+--   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1030+
1031+-- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
1032+-- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
1033+-- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
1034+-- for every occurrence of `X`.
1035+
1036+-- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
1037+-- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
1038+-- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
1039+-- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
1040+
1041+-- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
1042+-- We'll do that later in some exercises.
1043+
1044+-- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
1045+
1046+--   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
1047+--     X := X + 1
1048+--   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
1049+
1050+--   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
1051+--     X := 3
1052+--   {{ X = 3 }}
1053+
1054+--   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
1055+--     X := 3
1056+--   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
1057+
1058+-- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
1059+-- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
1060+-- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.subst`.
1061+
1062+-- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
1063+-- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
1064+-- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
1065+
1066+-- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
1067+-- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
1068+-- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
1069+-- directly "edit" its text.
1070+
1071+-- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
1072+-- state, defined as follows:
10971073 
10981074 def Assertion.subst (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
10991075   fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
11001076

1135+
1136+-- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
1137+-- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
1138+-- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
1139+
1140+-- To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with a
1141+-- couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that is,
1142+-- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1143+
1144+--   fun st =>
1145+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1146+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
1147+
1148+-- which simplifies to
1149+
1150+--   fun st =>
1151+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1152+--     (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
1153+
1154+-- and further simplifies to
1155+
1156+--   fun st =>
1157+--     ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
1158+
1159+-- and finally to
1160+
1161+--   fun st =>
1162+--     3 ≤ 5.
1163+
1164+-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5` (as
1165+-- expected).
1166+
1167+-- For a more interesting example, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦
1168+-- X + 1]`.
1169+-- Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1170+
1171+--   fun st =>
1172+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1173+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
1174+
1175+-- which simplifies to
1176+
1177+--   fun st =>
1178+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
1179+
1180+-- and further simplifies to
1181+
1182+--   fun st =>
1183+--     (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
1184+
1185+-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.

1321+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): hoare_asgn_fwd (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1322+
1323+-- By using a *parameter* `m` (a Lean number) to remember the original value
1324+-- of `X` we can define a Hoare rule for assignment that does, intuitively,
1325+-- "work forwards" rather than backwards.
1326+
1327+--   ------------------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_fwd)
1328+--   {{fun st => P st ∧ st[X] = m}}
1329+--     X := a
1330+--   {{fun st => P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧ st[X] = Aexp.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) a }}
1331+
1332+-- Note that we need to write out the postcondition in "desugared" form,
1333+-- because it needs to talk about two different states: we use the original
1334+-- value of `X` to reconstruct the state `st'` before the assignment took
1335+-- place. (Also note that this rule is more complicated than `hoare_asgn`!)
1336+
1337+-- Prove that this rule is correct.
1338+
1339+-- Note to developers:
1340+--     HIDE: BCP 21: Could we make the precondition use compact notation, at
1341+--     least?

1343+--     HIDE: SAZ 2024 - this version of the syntax does let us use the compact
1344+--     notation for the precondition, but it comes at the cost of having to
1345+--     "escape" the function in the postcondition.

1386+-- ### Consequence
1387+
1388+-- Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from the Hoare rules
1389+-- won't quite be the ones we want in the particular situation at hand -- they
1390+-- may be logically equivalent but have a different syntactic form that fails
1391+-- to unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they actually may be
1392+-- logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for postconditions) than
1393+-- what we need.
1394+
1395+-- For instance,
1396+
1397+--   {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1398+
1399+-- follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1400+
1401+--   {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1402+
1403+-- does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of `hoare_asgn`
1404+-- because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not syntactically equal
1405+-- assertions.
1406+
1407+-- However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple is valid, then
1408+-- the other must certainly be as well. We can capture this observation with
1409+-- the following rule:
1410+
1411+--      {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1412+--        P <<->> P'
1413+--   ---------------------
1414+--      {{P}} c {{Q}}
1415+
1416+-- Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that strengthening
1417+-- the precondition or weakening the postcondition of a valid triple always
1418+-- produces another valid triple. This observation is captured by two *Rules
1419+-- of Consequence*.
1420+
1421+--          {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1422+--             P ->> P'
1423+--   -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence_pre)
1424+--          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1425+
1426+--          {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1427+--            Q' ->> Q
1428+--   -----------------------------    (hoare_consequence_post)
1429+--          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1430+
1431+-- Here are the formal versions:
14611432 
14621433 theorem hoare_consequence_pre {P P' Q : Assertion} {c : Com}
14631434     (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
14771448   apply himp
14781449   exact hhoare heval hpre
14791450

1858+-- ### Conditionals
1859+
1860+-- What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional commands?
1861+
1862+-- Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing either of the
1863+-- branches, then it holds after the whole conditional. So we might be tempted
1864+-- to write:
1865+
1866+--           {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1867+--           {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1868+--   ---------------------------------
1869+--   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1870+
1871+-- However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule, we cannot show
1872+
1873+--   {{ True }}
1874+--     if X = 0
1875+--       then Y := 2
1876+--       else Y := X + 1
1877+--     end
1878+--   {{ X ≤ Y }}
1879+
1880+-- since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in which the
1881+-- assignments take place in the "then" and "else" branches.
1882+
1883+-- Fortunately, we can say something more precise. In the "then" branch, we
1884+-- know that the boolean expression `b` evaluates to `true`, and in the "else"
1885+-- branch, we know it evaluates to `false`. Making this information available
1886+-- in the premises of the rule gives us more information to work with when
1887+-- reasoning about the behavior of `c1` and `c2` (i.e., the reasons why they
1888+-- establish the postcondition `Q`).
1889+
1890+--   {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1891+--   {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1892+--   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1893+--   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1894+
1895+-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
1896+--     I have removed `bassertion` as it's an unnecessary abstraction and only
1897+--     adds overhead for the reader.
1898+--
1899+--     The following theorem is now unnecessary.

1914+-- Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for conditionals and prove it

1917+-- The statement of the rule reads: given `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}` and
1918+-- `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
1919+-- `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.

19601921 theorem hoare_if {P Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com}
19611922     (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
19691930     rw [← Bool.not_eq_true] at hb
19701931     exact hfalse hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩

2236+-- ### While Loops
2237+
2238+-- The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of a *command
2239+-- invariant* (or just *invariant*): an assertion whose truth is guaranteed
2240+-- after executing a command, assuming it is true before.
2241+
2242+-- That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c` if
2243+
2244+--   {{P}} c {{P}}
2245+
2246+-- holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily become false in
2247+-- the middle of executing `c`, but by the end of `c` it must be restored.
2248+
2249+-- As a first attempt at a `while` rule, we could try:
2250+
2251+--          {{P}} c {{P}}
2252+--   ---------------------------
2253+--   {{P}} while b do c end {{P}}
2254+
2255+-- This rule is valid: if `P` is a command invariant of `c`, as the premise
2256+-- requires, then, no matter how many times the loop body executes, `P` is
2257+-- going to be true when the loop finally finishes.
2258+
2259+-- But the rule also omits two crucial pieces of information. First, the loop
2260+-- terminates when `b` becomes false. So we can strengthen the postcondition
2261+-- in the conclusion:
22852262 
22862263 --           {{P}} c {{P}}
2287---    ---------------------------
2288---    {{P}} while b do c end {{P}}
2289-

2291---  premise requires, then, no matter how many times the loop body
2292---  executes, `P` is going to be true when the loop finally finishes.
2293-
2294---  But the rule also omits two crucial pieces of information. First, the
2295---  loop terminates when `b` becomes false. So we can strengthen the
2296---  postcondition in the conclusion:
2297-
2298---            {{P}} c {{P}}
2299---    ---------------------------------
2300---    {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2301-
2302---  Second, the loop body will be executed only if `b` is true. So we can
2303---  also strengthen the precondition in the premise:
2304-
2305---          {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2306---    --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
2307---    {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2308-
2309---  That is the Hoare `while` rule. Note how it combines aspects of `skip`
2310---  and conditionals:
2311-
2312---  - If the loop body executes zero times, the rule is like `skip` in that
2313---    the precondition survives to become (part of) the postcondition.
2314-
2315---  - Like a conditional, we can assume guard `b` holds on entry to the
2316---    subcommand.
2317-

2264+--   ---------------------------------
2265+--   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2266+
2267+-- Second, the loop body will be executed only if `b` is true. So we can also
2268+-- strengthen the precondition in the premise:
2269+
2270+--         {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2271+--   --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
2272+--   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2273+
2274+-- That is the Hoare `while` rule. Note how it combines aspects of `skip` and
2275+-- conditionals:
2276+
2277+-- - If the loop body executes zero times, the rule is like `skip` in that the
2278+--   precondition survives to become (part of) the postcondition.
2279+
2280+-- - Like a conditional, we can assume guard `b` holds on entry to the
2281+--   subcommand.

2330+-- We call `P` a *loop invariant* of `while b do c end` if
2331+
2332+--   {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2333+
2334+-- is a valid Hoare triple.
2335+
2336+-- This means that `P` will be true at the end of the loop body whenever the
2337+-- loop body executes. If `P` contradicts `b`, this holds trivially since the
2338+-- precondition is false.
2339+
2340+-- For instance, `X = 0` is a loop invariant of
2341+
2342+--   while X = 2 do X := 1 end
2343+
2344+-- since the program will never enter the loop.

2874+-- ## Summary
2875+
2876+-- So far, we've introduced Hoare Logic as a tool for reasoning about Imp
2877+-- programs.
2878+
2879+-- The rules of Hoare Logic are:
2880+
2881+--          --------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
2882+--          {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X:=a {{Q}}
2883+
2884+--          --------------------  (hoare_skip)
2885+--          {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
2886+
2887+--            {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
2888+--            {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
2889+--           ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
2890+--           {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
2891+
2892+--           {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
2893+--           {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
2894+--   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
2895+--   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
2896+
2897+--            {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2898+--     -----------------------------------  (hoare_while)
2899+--     {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬ b}}
2900+
2901+--             {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
2902+--                P ->> P'
2903+--                Q' ->> Q
2904+--      -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
2905+--             {{P}} c {{Q}}
2906+
2907+-- Our main task in this chapter has been to *define* the rules of Hoare
2908+-- logic, and prove that the definitions are sound. Having done so, we can go
2909+-- on and work *within* Hoare logic to prove that particular programs satisfy
2910+-- particular Hoare triples. In the next chapter, we'll see how Hoare logic is
2911+-- can be used to prove that more interesting programs satisfy interesting
2912+-- specifications of their behavior.
2913+
2914+-- Crucially, we will do so without ever again `unfold`ing the definition of
2915+-- Hoare triples -- i.e., we will take the rules of Hoare logic as a closed
2916+-- world for reasoning about programs.
2917+

114---  ## Decorated Programs
115-
116---  The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the
117---  structure of proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
118-
119---  We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
120---  low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
121---  appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
122-
123---  Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its
124---  own correctness.
125-
126---  For example, consider the program:
127-
128---    X := m;
129---    Z := p;
130---    while X <> 0 do
131---      Z := Z - 1;
132---      X := X - 1
133---    end
134-
135---  Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a
136---  Hoare triple:
137-
138---    {{ True }}
139---    X := m;
140---    Z := p;
141---    while X <> 0 do
142---      Z := Z - 1;
143---      X := X - 1
144---    end
145---    {{ Z = p - m }}
146-
147---  (Note the *parameters* `m` and `p`, which stand for fixed-but-arbitrary
148---  numbers. Formally, they are simply Lean variables of type `Nat`.)
149-
150---  Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a proof of this
151---  specification:
152-
153---    {{ True }} ->>
154---    {{ m = m }}
155---      X := m
156---                         {{ X = m }} ->>
157---                         {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
158---      Z := p;
159---                         {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
160---                         {{ Z - X = p - m }}
161---      while X <> 0 do
162---                         {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
163---                         {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
164---        Z := Z - 1
165---                         {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
166---        X := X - 1
167---                         {{ Z - X = p - m }}
168---      end
169---    {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
170---    {{ Z = p - m }}

195---  Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text
196---  interleaved with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by
197---  ->>).
198-
199---  A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a
200---  proof in Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify
201---  the Hoare triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of
202---  the Hoare Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows
203---  how to assemble all these individual steps into a proof for the whole
204---  program.
205-
206---  Our goal is to verify such decorated programs "mostly automatically."
207---  But, before we can verify anything, we need to be able to *find* a
208---  proof for a given specification, and for this we need to discover the
209---  right assertions. This can be done in an almost mechanical way, with
210---  the exception of finding loop invariants. In the remainder of this
211---  section, we explain in detail how to construct decorations for several
212---  short programs, all of which are loop free or have simple loop
213---  invariants. We'll return to finding more interesting loop invariants
214---  later in the chapter.

218---  Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
219---  using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary

223---    Y := X - Y;
224---    X := X - Y

226---  We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
227---  correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
228-
229---    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
230---    (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
231---             X := X + Y
232---    (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
233---             Y := X - Y
234---    (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
235---             X := X - Y
236---    (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}

238---  The decorations can be constructed as follows:
239-
240---  - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
241-
242---  - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
243---    postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n`
244---    to remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we
245---    can refer to them in the postcondition (5).
246-
247---  - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding

251---    obtain (4) by substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3)
252---    by substituting `Y` with `X - Y` in (4).

254---  - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the
255---    step from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by

109+-- ## Decorated Programs
110+
111+-- The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the structure of
112+-- proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
113+
114+-- We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
115+-- low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
116+-- appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
117+
118+-- Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its own
119+-- correctness.
120+
121+-- For example, consider the program:
122+
123+--   X := m;
124+--   Z := p;
125+--   while X <> 0 do
126+--     Z := Z - 1;
127+--     X := X - 1
128+--   end
129+
130+-- Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a Hoare
131+-- triple:
132+
133+--   {{ True }}
134+--   X := m;
135+--   Z := p;
136+--   while X <> 0 do
137+--     Z := Z - 1;
138+--     X := X - 1
139+--   end
140+--   {{ Z = p - m }}
141+
142+-- (Note the *parameters* `m` and `p`, which stand for fixed-but-arbitrary
143+-- numbers. Formally, they are simply Lean variables of type `Nat`.)
144+
145+-- Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a proof of this
146+-- specification:
147+
148+--   {{ True }} ->>
149+--   {{ m = m }}
150+--     X := m
151+--                        {{ X = m }} ->>
152+--                        {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
153+--     Z := p;
154+--                        {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
155+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
156+--     while X <> 0 do
157+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
158+--                        {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
159+--       Z := Z - 1
160+--                        {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
161+--       X := X - 1
162+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
163+--     end
164+--   {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
165+--   {{ Z = p - m }}
166+
167+-- Note to developers:
168+--     `HIDE: MRC'20: It bothers me a little in the proof above (and
169+--     similarly throughout the whole file really when it comes to guards)
170+--     that when we get to this part:
171+--     [[
172+--      while X <> 0 do {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
173+--     ]]
174+--     we are inconsistent about [X <> 0] vs. [~(X=0)].  I admit they
175+--     evaluate the same (er, sort of---the former is a [bexp] whereas the
176+--     latter is an assertion), but they aren't syntactically the same.
177+--     Since what we're teaching here (mechanized Hoare logic) is fussy
178+--     about syntax, it strikes me as something we ought to be precise
179+--     about. But it's an annoying change to propagate through the file,
180+--     so I haven't done it. Is it worth a comment, or do others not get
181+--     bothered by this?  Another way to fix this would be to add the [<>]
182+--     operator to Imp, so that we can write the guard in the nicer way.
183+--
184+--     BCP 20: I think adding in a few more boolean operators at the
185+--     outside is the way to go...
186+--
187+--     BCP 21: ... and I've now done this: <> is available in formal
188+--     bexps (also >).`
189+
190+-- Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text interleaved
191+-- with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by ->>).
192+
193+-- A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a proof in
194+-- Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify the Hoare
195+-- triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of the Hoare
196+-- Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows how to assemble
197+-- all these individual steps into a proof for the whole program.
198+
199+-- Our goal is to verify such decorated programs "mostly automatically." But,
200+-- before we can verify anything, we need to be able to *find* a proof for a
201+-- given specification, and for this we need to discover the right assertions.
202+-- This can be done in an almost mechanical way, with the exception of finding
203+-- loop invariants. In the remainder of this section, we explain in detail how
204+-- to construct decorations for several short programs, all of which are loop
205+-- free or have simple loop invariants. We'll return to finding more
206+-- interesting loop invariants later in the chapter.
207+
208+-- ### Example: Swapping
209+
210+-- Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
211+-- using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary
212+-- variable.
213+
214+--   X := X + Y;
215+--   Y := X - Y;
216+--   X := X - Y
217+
218+-- We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
219+-- correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
220+
221+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
222+--   (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
223+--            X := X + Y
224+--   (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
225+--            Y := X - Y
226+--   (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
227+--            X := X - Y
228+--   (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
229+
230+-- The decorations can be constructed as follows:
231+
232+-- - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
233+
234+-- - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
235+--   postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n` to
236+--   remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we can refer
237+--   to them in the postcondition (5).
238+
239+-- - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding until we
240+--   get to (2). At each step, we obtain the precondition of the assignment from
241+--   its postcondition by substituting the assigned variable with the
242+--   right-hand-side of the assignment. For instance, we obtain (4) by
243+--   substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3) by substituting `Y`
244+--   with `X - Y` in (4).
245+
246+-- - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the step
247+--   from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by doing a bit
248+--   of high-school algebra.
249+
250+-- Note to developers:
251+--     HIDE: BCP 21: This side comment seems too technical:
252+--
253+--     - (Note that we are working with natural numbers rather than fixed-width
254+--       machine integers, so we don't need to worry about the possibility of
255+--       arithmetic overflow anywhere in this argument. This makes life quite a
256+--       bit simpler!)
257+--
258+--     HIDE: A quick / optional exercise using just assignment here would be
259+--     good.
260+
261+-- ### Example: Simple Conditionals
262+
263+-- Here is a simple decorated program using conditionals:
264+
265+--   (1)   {{ True }}
266+--           if X <= Y then
267+--   (2)                    {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
268+--   (3)                    {{ (Y - X) + X = Y \/ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
269+--             Z := Y - X
270+--   (4)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
271+--           else
272+--   (5)                    {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
273+--   (6)                    {{ (X - Y) + X = Y \/ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
274+--             Z := X - Y
275+--   (7)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
276+--           end
277+--   (8)   {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
278+
279+-- These decorations can be constructed as follows:
280+
281+-- - We start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (8).
282+
283+-- - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_if` rule, we copy the
284+--   postcondition (8) to (4) and (7). We conjoin the precondition (1) with the
285+--   guard of the conditional to obtain (2). We conjoin (1) with the negated
286+--   guard of the conditional to obtain (5).
287+
288+-- - In order to use the assignment rule and obtain (3), we substitute `Z` by
289+--   `Y - X` in (4). To obtain (6) we substitute `Z` by `X - Y` in (7).
290+
291+-- - Finally, we verify that (2) implies (3) and (5) implies (6). Both of these
292+--   implications crucially depend on the ordering of `X` and `Y` obtained from
293+--   the guard. For instance, knowing that `X <= Y` ensures that subtracting `X`
294+--   from `Y` and then adding back `X` produces `Y`, as required by the first
295+--   disjunct of (3). Similarly, knowing that `~ (X <= Y)` ensures that
296+--   subtracting `Y` from `X` and then adding back `Y` produces `X`, as needed
297+--   by the second disjunct of (6). Note that `n - m + m = n` does *not* hold
298+--   for arbitrary natural numbers `n` and `m` (for example, [3 - 5 + 5 = 5]).
299+

379+-- ### Example: Division
380+
381+-- Let's do one more example of simple reasoning about a loop.
382+
383+-- The following Imp program calculates the integer quotient and remainder of
384+-- parameters `m` and `n`.
385+
386+--   X := m;
387+--   Y := 0;
388+--   while n <= X do
389+--     X := X - n;
390+--     Y := Y + 1
391+--   end;
392+
393+-- If we replace `m` and `n` by concrete numbers and execute the program, it
394+-- will terminate with the variable `X` set to the remainder when `m` is
395+-- divided by `n` and `Y` set to the quotient.
396+
397+-- In order to give a specification to this program we need to remember that
398+-- dividing `m` by `n` produces a remainder `X` and a quotient `Y` such that
399+-- `n * Y + X = m /\ X < n`.
400+
401+-- It turns out that we get lucky with this program and don't have to think
402+-- very hard about the loop invariant: the loop invariant is just the first
403+-- conjunct, `n * Y + X = m`, and we can use this to decorate the program.
404+
405+--    (1)  {{ True }} ->>
406+--    (2)  {{ n * 0 + m = m }}
407+--           X := m;
408+--    (3)                     {{ n * 0 + X = m }}
409+--           Y := 0;
410+--    (4)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
411+--           while n <= X do
412+--    (5)                     {{ n * Y + X = m /\ n <= X }} ->>
413+--    (6)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + (X - n) = m }}
414+--             X := X - n;
415+--    (7)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + X = m }}
416+--             Y := Y + 1
417+--    (8)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
418+--           end
419+--    (9)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ ~ (n <= X) }} ->>
420+--   (10)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ X < n }}
421+
422+-- Assertions (4), (5), (8), and (9) are derived mechanically from the loop
423+-- invariant and the loop's guard. Assertions (8), (7), and (6) are derived
424+-- using the assignment rule going backwards from (8) to (6). Assertions (4),
425+-- (3), and (2) are again backwards applications of the assignment rule.
426+
427+-- Now that we've decorated the program it only remains to check that the uses
428+-- of the consequence rule are correct — i.e., that (1) implies (2), that (5)
429+-- implies (6), and that (9) implies (10). This is indeed the case:
430+
431+-- - (1) ->> (2): trivial, by algebra.
432+
433+-- - (5) ->> (6): because `n <= X`, we are guaranteed that the subtraction in
434+--   (6) does not get zero-truncated. We can therefore rewrite (6) as
435+--   `n * Y + n + X - n` and cancel the `n`s, which results in the left conjunct
436+--   of (5).
437+
438+-- - (9) ->> (10): if `~ (n <= X)` then `X < n`. That's straightforward from
439+--   high-school algebra. So, we have a valid decorated program.
440+
441+-- ### From Decorated Programs to Formal Proofs
442+
443+-- From an informal proof in the form of a decorated program, it is "easy in
444+-- principle" to read off a formal proof using the Lean theorems corresponding
445+-- to the Hoare Logic rules, but these proofs can be a bit long and fiddly.
446+
447+-- Note that we do *not* unfold the definition of `ValidHoareTriple` anywhere
448+-- in this proof: the point of the game we're playing now is to use the Hoare
449+-- rules as a self-contained logic for reasoning about programs.

491+-- ## Formal Decorated Programs
492+
493+-- Our informal conventions for decorated programs amount to a way of
494+-- "displaying" Hoare triples, in which commands are annotated with enough
495+-- embedded assertions that checking the validity of a triple is reduced to
496+-- simple logical and algebraic calculations showing that some assertions
497+-- imply others.
498+
499+-- In this section, we show that this presentation style can be made
500+-- completely formal — and indeed that checking the validity of decorated
501+-- programs can be largely automated.
502+
503+-- ### Syntax
504+
505+-- The first thing we need to do is to formalize a variant of the syntax of
506+-- Imp commands that includes embedded assertions, which we'll call
507+-- "decorations." We call the new commands *decorated commands*, or `dcom`s.
508+
509+-- The choice of exactly where to put assertions in the definition of `dcom`
510+-- is a bit subtle. The simplest thing to do would be to annotate every `dcom`
511+-- with a precondition and postcondition — something like this...

533+-- But this would result in *very* verbose decorated programs with a lot of
534+-- repeated annotations: a simple program like `skip;skip` would be decorated
535+-- like this,
536+
537+--   {{P}} ({{P}} skip {{P}}) ; ({{P}} skip {{P}}) {{P}}
538+
539+-- with pre- and post-conditions around each `skip`, plus identical pre- and
540+-- post-conditions on the semicolon!
541+
542+-- In other words, we don't want both preconditions and postconditions on each
543+-- command, because a sequence of two commands would contain redundant
544+-- decorations — the postcondition of the first likely being the same as the
545+-- precondition of the second.
546+
547+-- Instead, our formal syntax of decorated commands will omit preconditions
548+-- whenever possible and embed just postconditions.
549+
550+-- - The `skip` command, for example, is decorated only with its postcondition
551+
552+--   skip {{ Q }}
553+
554+-- on the assumption that the precondition will be provided by somebody else.
555+
556+-- We carry the same assumption through the other syntactic forms: each
557+-- decorated command is assumed to carry its own postcondition within itself
558+-- but take its precondition from its context in which it is used.
559+
560+-- - Sequences `d1 ; d2` need no additional decorations.
561+
562+-- Why?
563+
564+-- Because inside `d2` there will be a postcondition, which also serves as the
565+-- postcondition of `d1;d2`.
566+
567+-- Similarly, inside `d1` there will also be a postcondition, which
568+-- additionally serves as the *precondition* for `d2`.
569+
570+-- - An assignment `X := a` is decorated only with its postcondition:
571+
572+--   X := a {{ Q }}
573+
574+-- - A conditional `if b then d1 else d2` is decorated with a postcondition for
575+--   the entire statement, as well as preconditions for each branch:
576+
577+--   if b then {{ P1 }} d1 else {{ P2 }} d2 end {{ Q }}
578+
579+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
580+--     Maybe we need a note here about why we don't just calculate P1 and P2
581+--     later, once we know the precondition of the whole loop. Indeed, we
582+--     could (and perhaps should, as discussed elsewhere), but we are doing
583+--     something simpler for the moment.
584+
585+-- - A loop `while b do d end` is decorated with its final postcondition plus a
586+--   precondition for the body:
587+
588+--   while b do {{ P }} d end {{ Q }}
589+
590+-- The postcondition embedded in `d` serves as the loop invariant.
591+
592+-- - Implications `->>` can be added as decorations either for a precondition...
593+
594+--   ->> {{ P }} d
595+
596+-- ...or for a postcondition:
597+
598+--   d ->> {{ Q }}
599+
600+-- The former is waiting for another precondition to be supplied by the
601+-- context; the latter relies on the postcondition already embedded in `d`.
602+
603+-- Putting this all together gives us the formal syntax of decorated commands:
627604 
628605 inductive DCom where
629606   | skip (post : Assertion)
638615   | pre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
639616   | post (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)

796+-- The outer Hoare triple of a decorated program is just a `Prop`; thus, to
797+-- show that it is *valid*, we need to produce a proof of this proposition.
798+
799+-- We will do this by extracting "proof obligations" from the decorations
800+-- sprinkled throughout the program.
801+
802+-- These obligations are often called *verification conditions*, because they
803+-- are the facts that must be verified to see that the decorations are locally
804+-- consistent and thus constitute a proof of validity of the outer triple.
805+
806+-- ### Extracting Verification Conditions
807+
808+-- The function `DCom.VerificationConditions` takes a decorated command `d`
809+-- together with a precondition `P` and returns a *proposition* that, if it
810+-- can be proved, implies that the triple
811+
812+--   {{P}} d.erase {{d.postcondition}}
813+
814+-- is valid.
815+
816+-- It does this by walking over `d` and generating a big conjunction that
817+-- includes
818+
819+-- - local consistency checks for each form of command, plus
820+
821+-- - uses of `->>` to bridge the gap between the assertions found inside a
822+--   decorated command and the assertions imposed by the external precondition;
823+--   these uses correspond to applications of the consequence rule.
824+
825+-- *Local consistency* is defined as follows...
826+
827+-- - The decorated command
828+
829+--   skip {{Q}}
830+
831+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if `P ->> Q`.
832+
833+-- - The sequential composition of `d1` and `d2` is locally consistent with
834+--   respect to `P` if `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P` and `d2`
835+--   is locally consistent with respect to the postcondition of `d1`.
836+
837+-- - An assignment
838+
839+--   X := a {{Q}}
840+
841+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
842+
843+--   P ->> Q [X |-> a]
844+
845+-- - A conditional
846+
847+--   if b then {{P1}} d1 else {{P2}} d2 end {{Q}}
848+
849+-- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if
850+
851+-- (1) `P /\ b ->> P1`
852+
853+-- (2) `P /\ ~b ->> P2`
854+
855+-- (3) `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P1`
856+
857+-- (4) `d2` is locally consistent with respect to `P2`
858+
859+-- (5) `d1.postcondition ->> Q`
860+
861+-- (6) `d2.postcondition ->> Q`
862+
863+-- - A loop
864+
865+--   while b do {{Q}} d end {{R}}
866+
867+-- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if:
868+
869+-- (1) `P ->> d.postcondition`
870+
871+-- (2) `d.postcondition /\ b ->> Q`
872+
873+-- (3) `d.postcondition /\ ~b ->> R`
874+
875+-- (4) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
876+
877+-- - A command with an extra assertion at the beginning
878+
879+--   ->> {{Q}} d
880+
881+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
882+
883+-- (1) `P ->> Q`
884+
885+-- (2) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
886+
887+-- - A command with an extra assertion at the end
888+
889+--   d ->> {{Q}}
890+
891+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
892+
893+-- (1) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
894+
895+-- (2) `d.postcondition ->> Q`
896+
897+-- With all this in mind, we can write a *verification condition generator*
898+-- that takes a decorated command and reads off a proposition saying that all
899+-- its decorations are locally consistent.
900+
901+-- Formally, since a decorated command is "waiting for its precondition" the
902+-- main VC generator takes a `dcom` plus a given precondition as arguments.
903+
904+-- Note to developers:
905+--     HIDE: There was some discussion in 2016 about whether the VC generator
906+--     should should use equivalence or implication in a few places. I (BCP)
907+--     believe Phil (Wadler) changed some instances of the former to the
908+--     latter.
909+--
910+--     HIDE: MRC'20: a written explanation of each part of this would be quite
911+--     nice. BCP 21: Agreed!! (BCP 23: But it's kind of what's just above...)
941912 
942913 def DCom.VerificationConditions
943914     (P : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
969940       body.VerificationConditions P ∧
970941       (body.postcondition ->> Q)
971942

974---  plays a critical role at some point in the proof.

975946 
976947 theorem verification_correct (d : DCom) (P : Assertion)
977948     (hvc : d.VerificationConditions P) :
978949     ValidHoareTriple P d.erase d.postcondition := by
979950   sorry
980951

992963     dec.OuterTripleValid := by
993964   exact verification_correct dec.body dec.pre hvc

1124---  ## Finding Loop Invariants
1125-
1126---  Once the outermost precondition and postcondition are chosen, the only
1127---  creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the
1128---  right loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the
1129---  reason that inductive mathematical proofs are:
1130-
1131---  - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger
1132---    assumption to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of
1133---    the loop body, but it also means that the loop body's postcondition
1134---    is harder to prove.
1135-
1136---  - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you
1137---    have a stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the
1138---    induction step of the proof, but it also means that the statement
1139---    being proved inductively is harder to prove.
1140-
1141---  This section explains how to approach the challenge of finding loop
1142---  invariants through a series of examples and exercises.
1143-
1144---  ### Example: Slow Subtraction
1145-
1146---  The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the value of `Y`
1147---  by repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We want to verify its
1148---  correctness with respect to the pre- and postconditions shown:
1149-
1150---    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
1151---      while X <> 0 do
1152---        Y := Y - 1;
1153---        X := X - 1
1154---      end
1155---    {{ Y = n - m }}
1156-
1157---  To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv` for the
1158---  loop. As a first step we can leave `Inv` as an unknown and build a
1159---  *skeleton* for the proof by applying the rules for local consistency,
1160---  working from the end of the program to the beginning, as usual, and
1161---  without doing any thinking at all yet.
1162-
1163---  This leads to the following skeleton:
1164-
1165---    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
1166---    (2)    {{ Inv }}
1167---             while X <> 0 do
1168---    (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
1169---    (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
1170---               Y := Y - 1;
1171---    (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
1172---               X := X - 1
1173---    (6)              {{ Inv }}
1174---             end
1175---    (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
1176---    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1177-
1178---  Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
1179---  respect three conditions:
1180-
1181---  - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's
1182---    precondition, i.e., (1) must imply (2);
1183-
1184---  - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's postcondition,
1185---    i.e., (7) must imply (8);
1186-
1187---  - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the loop,
1188---    assuming that the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must
1189---    imply (4).
1190-
1191---  These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
1192---  specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy
1193---  them.
1194-
1195---  One way to find a loop invariant that simultaneously satisfies these
1196---  three conditions is by using an iterative process: start with a
1197---  "candidate" invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check
1198---  the three conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the
1199---  information that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully
1200---  better — candidate invariant, and repeat.
1201-
1202---  For instance, in the reduce-to-zero example above, we saw that, for a
1203---  very simple loop, choosing `True` as a loop invariant did the job.
1204---  Maybe it will work here too. To find out, let's try instantiating `Inv`
1205---  with `True` in the skeleton above and see what we get...
