1095+-- ## Finding Loop Invariants
1096+
1097+-- Once the outermost precondition and postcondition are chosen, the only
1098+-- creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the right
1099+-- loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the reason
1100+-- that inductive mathematical proofs are:
1101+
1102+-- - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger assumption
1103+--   to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of the loop body,
1104+--   but it also means that the loop body's postcondition is harder to prove.
1105+
1106+-- - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you have a
1107+--   stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the induction step
1108+--   of the proof, but it also means that the statement being proved inductively
1109+--   is harder to prove.
1110+
1111+-- This section explains how to approach the challenge of finding loop
1112+-- invariants through a series of examples and exercises.
1113+
1114+-- ### Example: Slow Subtraction
1115+
1116+-- The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the value of `Y` by
1117+-- repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We want to verify its correctness
1118+-- with respect to the pre- and postconditions shown:
1119+
1120+--   {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
1121+--     while X <> 0 do
1122+--       Y := Y - 1;
1123+--       X := X - 1
1124+--     end
1125+--   {{ Y = n - m }}
1126+
1127+-- To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv` for the loop. As
1128+-- a first step we can leave `Inv` as an unknown and build a *skeleton* for
1129+-- the proof by applying the rules for local consistency, working from the end
1130+-- of the program to the beginning, as usual, and without doing any thinking
1131+-- at all yet.
1132+
1133+-- This leads to the following skeleton:
1134+
1135+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
1136+--   (2)    {{ Inv }}
1137+--            while X <> 0 do
1138+--   (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
1139+--   (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
1140+--              Y := Y - 1;
1141+--   (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
1142+--              X := X - 1
1143+--   (6)              {{ Inv }}
1144+--            end
1145+--   (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
1146+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1147+
1148+-- Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
1149+-- respect three conditions:
1150+
1151+-- - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's precondition,
1152+--   i.e., (1) must imply (2);
1153+
1154+-- - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's postcondition, i.e.,
1155+--   (7) must imply (8);
1156+
1157+-- - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the loop, assuming that
1158+--   the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must imply (4).
1159+
1160+-- These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
1161+-- specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy them.
1162+
1163+-- One way to find a loop invariant that simultaneously satisfies these three
1164+-- conditions is by using an iterative process: start with a "candidate"
1165+-- invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check the three
1166+-- conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the information
1167+-- that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully better —
1168+-- candidate invariant, and repeat.
1169+
1170+-- For instance, in the reduce-to-zero example above, we saw that, for a very
1171+-- simple loop, choosing `True` as a loop invariant did the job. Maybe it will
1172+-- work here too. To find out, let's try instantiating `Inv` with `True` in
1173+-- the skeleton above and see what we get...
1174+
1175+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                    (a - OK)
1176+--   (2)    {{ True }}
1177+--            while X <> 0 do
1178+--   (3)                   {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>     (c - OK)
1179+--   (4)                   {{ True }}
1180+--              Y := Y - 1;
1181+--   (5)                   {{ True }}
1182+--              X := X - 1
1183+--   (6)                   {{ True }}
1184+--            end
1185+--   (7)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                 (b - WRONG!)
1186+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1187+
1188+-- While conditions (a) and (c) are trivially satisfied, (b) is wrong: it is
1189+-- not the case that `True /\ X = 0` (7) implies `Y = n - m` (8). In fact, the
1190+-- two assertions are completely unrelated, so it is very easy to find a
1191+-- counterexample to the implication (say, `Y = X = m = 0` and `n = 1`).
1192+
1193+-- If we want (b) to hold, we need to strengthen the loop invariant so that it
1194+-- implies the postcondition (8). One simple way to do this is to let the loop
1195+-- invariant *be* the postcondition. So let's return to our skeleton,
1196+-- instantiate `Inv` with `Y = n - m`, and try checking conditions (a) to (c)
1197+-- again.
1198+
1199+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                        (a - WRONG!)
1200+--   (2)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1201+--            while X <> 0 do
1202+--   (3)                     {{ Y = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>  (c - WRONG!)
1203+--   (4)                     {{ Y - 1 = n - m }}
1204+--              Y := Y - 1;
1205+--   (5)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1206+--              X := X - 1
1207+--   (6)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1208+--            end
1209+--   (7)    {{ Y = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1210+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1211+
1212+-- This time, condition (b) holds trivially, but (a) and (c) are broken.
1213+-- Condition (a) requires that (1) `X = m /\ Y = n` implies (2) `Y = n - m`.
1214+-- If we substitute `Y` by `n` we have to show that `n = n - m` for arbitrary
1215+-- `m` and `n`, which is not the case (for instance, when `m = n = 1`).
1216+-- Condition (c) requires that `n - m - 1 = n - m`, which fails, for instance,
1217+-- for `n = 1` and `m = 0`. So, although `Y = n - m` holds at the end of the
1218+-- loop, it does not hold from the start, and it doesn't hold on each
1219+-- iteration; it is not a correct loop invariant.
1220+
1221+-- This failure is not very surprising: the variable `Y` changes during the
1222+-- loop, while `m` and `n` are constant, so the assertion we chose didn't have
1223+-- much chance of being a loop invariant!
1224+
1225+-- To do better, we need to generalize (7) to some statement that is
1226+-- equivalent to (8) when `X` is `0`, since this will be the case when the
1227+-- loop terminates, and that "fills the gap" in some appropriate way when `X`
1228+-- is nonzero. Looking at how the loop works, we can observe that `X` and `Y`
1229+-- are decremented together until `X` reaches `0`. So, if `X = 2` and `Y = 5`
1230+-- initially, after one iteration of the loop we obtain `X = 1` and `Y = 4`;
1231+-- after two iterations `X = 0` and `Y = 3`; and then the loop stops. Notice
1232+-- that the difference between `Y` and `X` stays constant between iterations:
1233+-- initially, `Y = n` and `X = m`, and the difference is always `n - m`. So
1234+-- let's try instantiating `Inv` in the skeleton above with `Y - X = n - m`.
1235+
1236+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                            (a - OK)
1237+--   (2)    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1238+--            while X <> 0 do
1239+--   (3)                    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>   (c - OK)
1240+--   (4)                    {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1241+--              Y := Y - 1;
1242+--   (5)                    {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1243+--              X := X - 1
1244+--   (6)                    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1245+--            end
1246+--   (7)    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1247+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1248+
1249+-- Success! Conditions (a), (b) and (c) all hold now. (To verify (c), we need
1250+-- to check that, under the assumption that `X <> 0`, we have
1251+-- `Y - X = (Y - 1) - (X - 1)`; this holds for all natural numbers `X` and
1252+-- `Y`.)
1253+
1254+-- Here is the final version of the decorated program:

12921257   pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
13061271     (subtractSlowlyDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by

1551+--   (5)            {{ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=m /\ m<((Z+1)+1)*((Z+1)+1) }}
1552+--             Z := Z+1

1556+--   (8)  {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}

1559+-- condition (c), we see that the second conjunct of (4) is almost the same as

2715+-- ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
2716+
2717+-- Note to developers:
2718+--     HIDE: BCP 21: We talked about moving this stuff to the HoareAsLogic
2719+--     chapter to lighten this chapter, but it fits awkwardly there, so I'm
2720+--     leaving it here. It's optional anyway. We might consider assigning one
2721+--     of the exercises as advanced-only though.
2722+
2723+-- Some preconditions are more interesting than others. For example, the Hoare
2724+-- triple
2725+
2726+--   {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2727+
2728+-- is *not* very interesting: although it is perfectly valid, it tells us
2729+-- nothing useful. Since the precondition isn't satisfied by any state, it
2730+-- doesn't describe any situations where we can use the command `X := Y + 1`
2731+-- to achieve the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2732+
2733+-- By contrast,
2734+
2735+--   {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
2736+
2737+-- has a useful precondition: it tells us that, if we can somehow create a
2738+-- situation in which we know that `Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0`, then running this
2739+-- command will produce a state satisfying the postcondition. However, this
2740+-- precondition is not as useful as it could be, because the `Z = 0` clause in
2741+-- the precondition actually has nothing to do with the postcondition
2742+-- `X <= 5`.
2743+
2744+-- The *most* useful precondition for this command is this one:
2745+
2746+--   {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2747+
2748+-- The assertion `Y <= 4` is called the *weakest precondition* of `X := Y + 1`
2749+-- with respect to the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2750+
2751+-- Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command `X := Y + 1` with
2752+-- respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as meaning
2753+-- "easiest to satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as many states as
2754+-- possible can satisfy.
2755+
2756+-- `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for postcondition `Q` if
2757+
2758+-- - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
2759+
2760+-- - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is, if
2761+--   `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
2762+
2763+-- Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For example, `Y <= 4`
2764+-- was a weakest precondition above, but so are the logically equivalent
2765+-- assertions `Y < 5`, `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show that any two
2766+-- weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with respect to
2767+-- postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is, `P <<->> P'`.
28062768 
28072769 def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
28082770   ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
2809-  ∀ P' : Assertion, {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }} → P' ->> P

37+-- In this chapter, we take a more serious look at how to use Lean as a tool
38+-- to study other things. Our case study is a *simple imperative programming
39+-- language* called Imp, embodying a tiny core fragment of conventional
40+-- mainstream languages such as C and Java.
41+
42+-- Here is a familiar mathematical function written in Imp.
43+
44+--   Z := X;
45+--   Y := 1;
46+--   while (Z ≠ 0) {
47+--     Y := Y * Z;
48+--     Z := Z - 1;
49+--   }
50+
51+-- We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics* of Imp; later
52+-- in this volume we develop a theory of *program equivalence* and introduce
53+-- *Hoare Logic*, a popular logic for reasoning about imperative programs.
54+
55+-- We build Imp in three layers. The first — a core language of *arithmetic
56+-- and boolean expressions* — is developed in its own chapter, *Slang*; read
57+-- that one first. There you meet the abstract syntax of arithmetic
58+-- expressions (`Aexp`) and boolean expressions (`Bexp`), their evaluation
59+-- both as a recursive *function* and as an inductive *relation* (proved
60+-- equivalent), and a small `optimize0plus` program transformation together
61+-- with its correctness proof. Those expressions are *variable-free*.
62+
63+-- This chapter picks up from there. First we extend the expressions with
64+-- *variables*; then we add a language of *commands* — assignment,
65+-- conditionals, sequencing, and loops.
66+
67+-- ## Expressions With Variables
68+
69+-- Let's return to defining Imp. The next thing we need to do is to enrich our
70+-- arithmetic and boolean expressions with variables. To keep things simple,
71+-- we'll assume that all variables are global and that they only hold numbers.
72+
73+-- ### States
74+
75+-- Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their current values,
76+-- we'll use total maps from the `Maps` chapter. A *machine state* (or just
77+-- *state*) represents the current values of all variables at some point in
78+-- the execution of a program.
79+
80+-- For simplicity, we assume that the state is defined for *all* variables,
81+-- even though any given program is only able to mention a finite number of
82+-- them. Because each variable stores a natural number, we represent the state
83+-- as a total map from strings (variable names) to `Nat`, and will use `0` as
84+-- the default value in the store.
85+
86+-- We give the type of variable identifiers a name, `Ident`. For now it is
87+-- just `String`; naming it makes the intent clearer.

152---  ### Notations
153-
154---  To make Imp programs easier to read and write, we introduce some
155---  notations.
156-
157---  You do not need to understand exactly what these declarations do.
158---  Briefly, though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:
159-
160---  - The `declare_syntax_cat` directive adds a new non-terminal to Lean's
161---    grammar, called `imp_aexp`. We'll add additional non-terminals
162---    further below.
163-
164---  - Each `syntax` directive defines a grammar production, of which there
165---    are eight in total. The first two define literals, `num` and `ident`,
166---    as `imp_aexp`s. The next several directives define productions for
167---    building larger expressions, with some annotations to define
168---    precedence, etc.
169-
170---  - Finally, `macro_rules` is used to translate each production of the
171---    `imp_aexp` nonterminal into a Lean expression.
172-
173---  Boolean expressions and, later, commands follow this same pattern
174---  exactly, so their declarations are collapsed where they appear: open

146+-- ### Notations
147+
148+-- To make Imp programs easier to read and write, we introduce some notations.
149+
150+-- You do not need to understand exactly what these declarations do. Briefly,
151+-- though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:
152+
153+-- - The `declare_syntax_cat` directive adds a new non-terminal to Lean's
154+--   grammar, called `imp_aexp`. We'll add additional non-terminals further
155+--   below.
156+
157+-- - Each `syntax` directive defines a grammar production, of which there are
158+--   eight in total. The first two define literals, `num` and `ident`, as
159+--   `imp_aexp`s. The next several directives define productions for building
160+--   larger expressions, with some annotations to define precedence, etc.
161+
162+-- - Finally, `macro_rules` is used to translate each production of the
163+--   `imp_aexp` nonterminal into a Lean expression.
164+
165+-- Boolean expressions and, later, commands follow this same pattern exactly,
166+-- so their declarations are collapsed where they appear: open one if you want
167+-- to see the pattern repeated, and skip them otherwise.

262---  ### Delaborators
263-
264---  The notations above are *input* only: they teach Lean how to **read**
265---  `aexp
266---  { … }` and `bexp { … }`, but Lean still **prints** an expression
267---  using its raw constructors -- `example_aexp` shows up as
268---  `Aexp.plus (Aexp.num 3) …` rather than `aexp { 3 + X * 2 }`. A
269---  *delaborator* closes the loop. Where a `macro` turns surface syntax
270---  into a term (*elaboration*), a delaborator does the reverse: it turns
271---  an elaborated term back into surface syntax so that Lean's own output
272---  uses our concrete Imp notation.
273-
274---  Each delaborator walks a term of the given type and rebuilds the
275---  matching piece of `imp_aexp`/`imp_bexp` syntax; a subterm Lean doesn't
276---  recognize is printed with the `~` escape. The `@[delab …]` attribute
277---  registers the top-level function to fire whenever Lean is about to
278---  display a term headed by one of those constructors -- unless notation
279---  printing has been switched off with `set_option pp.notation false`,
280---  which lets us fall back to the raw constructors when debugging (see
281---  *Desugaring Notations* below). The companion *category parenthesizer*
282---  re-inserts the parentheses the grammar's precedences demand, so that,
283---  e.g., `(1 + 2) * 3` prints with its parentheses intact.

288---  syntax rather than as a pile of constructors.

250+-- ### Delaborators
251+
252+-- The notations above are *input* only: they teach Lean how to **read**
253+-- `aexp
254+-- { … }` and `bexp { … }`, but Lean still **prints** an expression
255+-- using its raw constructors -- `example_aexp` shows up as
256+-- `Aexp.plus (Aexp.num 3) …` rather than `aexp { 3 + X * 2 }`. A
257+-- *delaborator* closes the loop. Where a `macro` turns surface syntax into a
258+-- term (*elaboration*), a delaborator does the reverse: it turns an
259+-- elaborated term back into surface syntax so that Lean's own output uses our
260+-- concrete Imp notation.
261+
262+-- Each delaborator walks a term of the given type and rebuilds the matching
263+-- piece of `imp_aexp`/`imp_bexp` syntax; a subterm Lean doesn't recognize is
264+-- printed with the `~` escape. The `@[delab …]` attribute registers the
265+-- top-level function to fire whenever Lean is about to display a term headed
266+-- by one of those constructors -- unless notation printing has been switched
267+-- off with `set_option pp.notation false`, which lets us fall back to the raw
268+-- constructors when debugging (see *Desugaring Notations* below). The
269+-- companion *category parenthesizer* re-inserts the parentheses the grammar's
270+-- precedences demand, so that, e.g., `(1 + 2) * 3` prints with its
271+-- parentheses intact.
272+
273+-- You do not need to understand the details, and the code is collapsed below
274+-- for that reason. The result is that a `#check`, an `#eval`, or a proof goal
275+-- mentioning an Imp expression is displayed in readable Imp syntax rather
276+-- than as a pile of constructors.

500+-- Now we are ready to define the syntax and behavior of Imp *commands* (or

674---  ### Desugaring Notations
675-
676---  The `imp { … }` notation, together with the delaborators, is purely a
677---  convenience for reading and writing programs. Occasionally, such as
678---  when debugging a definition or a stuck proof, the concrete syntax
679---  `hide`s the underlying structure we want to see. For those moments we
680---  can switch the Imp notation off in Lean's output with
681---  `set_option pp.notation false`, which our delaborators honor.
682-
683---  Note that unlike a `def`, `imp { … }` is a `macro` which is expanded
684---  during elaboration, **before** the resulting term is type-checked. So
685---  `fact_in_lean` is not a program hidden behind a layer of notation that
686---  a proof must first peel back; it simply **is** the underlying tree of
687---  `Com`, `Aexp`, and `Bexp` constructors. Consequently, when a proof goal
688---  mentions an Imp program, tactics such as `cases`, `injection`, and
689---  `simp` already act on those constructors directly -- there is nothing
690---  to "unfold". The delaborators affect only how that tree is
691---  **displayed**. Nevertheless, seeing the raw constructors is sometimes
692---  very helpful!

774+-- ### Evaluation as a Relation
775+
776+-- Here's a better way: define `ceval` as a *relation* rather than a
777+-- *function* -- i.e., make its result a `Prop` rather than a `State`, similar
778+-- to what we did for `Aexp.EvalR` above.
779+
780+-- This is an important change. Besides freeing us from awkward workarounds,
781+-- it gives us more flexibility in the definition. For example, if we add
782+-- nondeterministic features like `any` to the language, we want the
783+-- definition of evaluation to be nondeterministic -- i.e., not only will it
784+-- not be total, it will not even be a function!
785+
786+-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
787+--     I kind of hate this notation. Is there something more standard in Lean?
788+--     CSLib precedent maybe?
789+
790+-- We'll use the notation `st =[ c ]=> st'` for the `Com.EvalR` relation:
791+-- `st =[ c ]=> st'` means that executing program `c` in a starting state `st`
792+-- results in an ending state `st'`. This can be pronounced "`c` takes state
793+-- `st` to `st'`".
794+
795+-- Operational Semantics
796+
797+-- Note to developers (before next release):
798+--     BCP 21: I wonder if `seq` would be easier to work with if st' and st''
799+--     were swapped...
800+
801+-- Here is an informal definition of evaluation, presented as inference rules
802+-- for readability:
803+
804+--                         -----------------                  (skip)
805+--                         st =[ skip ]=> st
806+
807+--                         a.eval st = n
808+--                 --------------------------------           (asgn)
809+--                 st =[ x := a ]=> (x →ₜ n ; st)
810+
811+--                         st  =[ c1 ]=> st'
812+--                         st' =[ c2 ]=> st''
813+--                       ---------------------                (seq)
814+--                       st =[ c1;c2 ]=> st''
815+
816+--                        b.eval st = true
817+--                         st =[ c1 ]=> st'
818+--              --------------------------------------        (ifTrue)
819+--              st =[ if b then c1 else c2 end ]=> st'
820+
821+--                       b.eval st = false
822+--                         st =[ c2 ]=> st'
823+--              --------------------------------------        (ifFalse)
824+--              st =[ if b then c1 else c2 end ]=> st'
825+
826+--                       b.eval st = false
827+--                  -----------------------------             (whileFalse)
828+--                  st =[ while b do c end ]=> st
829+
830+--                        b.eval st = true
831+--                         st =[ c ]=> st'
832+--                st' =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
833+--                --------------------------------            (whileTrue)
834+--                st  =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
835+
836+-- Here is the formal definition. Make sure you understand how it corresponds
837+-- to the inference rules.

1011---  ### Determinism of Evaluation
1012-
1013---  Changing from a computational to a relational definition of evaluation
1014---  is a good move because it frees us from the artificial requirement that
1015---  evaluation be a total function. But it raises a question: is the
1016---  relational definition really a partial *function*? Could the same
1017---  command, from the same state, evaluate to two different final states?
1018---  In fact this cannot happen: `ceval` *is* a partial function.

1280-
1281---  The goal of this exercise is to write a small compiler that translates
1282---  `aexp`s into stack machine instructions.
1283-
1284---  The instruction set for our stack language will consist of the
1285---  following instructions:
1286-
1287---  - `sPush n`: Push the number `n` on the stack.
1288-
1289---  - `sLoad x`: Load the identifier `x` from the store and push it on the
1290---    stack
1291-
1292---  - `sPlus`: Pop the two top numbers from the stack, add them, and push
1293---    the result onto the stack.
1294-
1295---  - `sMinus`: Similar, but subtract the first number from the second.
1296-
1297---  - `sMult`: Similar, but multiply.
1298-
1299-namespace StackCompiler
1300-
1301-inductive Sinstr : Type where
1302-| sPush (n : Nat)
1303-| sLoad (x : String)
1304-| sPlus
1305-| sMinus
1306-| sMult
1307-
1308-open Sinstr
1309-
1310---  Write a function to evaluate programs in the stack language. It should
1311---  take as input a state, a stack represented as a list of numbers (top
1312---  stack item is the head of the list), and a program represented as a
1313---  list of instructions, and it should return the stack after executing
1314---  the program. Test your function on the examples below.
1315-
1316---  Note that it is unspecified what to do when encountering an `sPlus`,
1317---  `sMinus`, or `sMult` instruction if the stack contains fewer than two
1318---  elements. In a sense, it is immaterial what we do, since a correct
1319---  compiler will never emit such a malformed program. But for sake of
1320---  later exercises, it would be best to skip the offending instruction and
1321---  continue with the next one.
1322-
1323-def sExecute (st : State) (stack : List Nat) (prog : List Sinstr) : List Nat :=
1324-  (match prog, stack with
1325-    | [],                _           => stack
1326-    | sPush n :: prog',  _            => sExecute st (n       :: stack)  prog'
1327-    | sLoad x :: prog',  _            => sExecute st (st[x]   :: stack)  prog'
1328-    | sPlus   :: prog',  n::m::stack' => sExecute st ((m + n) :: stack') prog'
1329-    | sMinus  :: prog',  n::m::stack' => sExecute st ((m - n) :: stack') prog'
1330-    | sMult   :: prog',  n::m::stack' => sExecute st ((m * n) :: stack') prog'
1331-    | _       :: prog',  _            => sExecute st stack prog')
1332-                                        -- Bad state: skip
1333-
1334-@[simp] theorem sExecute_nil {st : State} {stack : List Nat}
1335-  : sExecute st stack [] = stack := rfl
1336-@[simp] theorem sExecute_push {n : Nat} {st : State} {stack : List Nat} {prog' : List Sinstr} :
1337-  sExecute st stack (sPush n :: prog') = sExecute st (n :: stack) prog' := rfl
1338-@[simp] theorem sExecute_load {x : String} {st : State} {stack : List Nat} {prog' : List Sinstr} :
1339-  sExecute st stack (sLoad x :: prog') = sExecute st (st[x] :: stack) prog' := rfl
1340-@[simp] theorem sExecute_plus {n m : Nat} {st : State} {stack' : List Nat}
1341-  {prog' : List Sinstr} :
1342-  sExecute st (n :: m :: stack') (sPlus :: prog') = sExecute st ((m + n) :: stack') prog' := rfl
1343-@[simp] theorem sExecute_minus {n m : Nat} {st : State} {stack' : List Nat}
1344-  {prog' : List Sinstr} :
1345-  sExecute st (n :: m :: stack') (sMinus :: prog') = sExecute st ((m - n) :: stack') prog' := rfl
1346-@[simp] theorem sExecute_mult {n m : Nat}  {st : State} {stack' : List Nat}
1347-  {prog' : List Sinstr} :
1348-   sExecute st (n :: m :: stack') (sMult :: prog') = sExecute st ((m * n) :: stack') prog' := rfl
1349-@[simp] theorem sExecute_plus_bad {st : State} {stack : List Nat} {prog' : List Sinstr}
1350-  (hs : stack.length < 2) :
1351-  sExecute st stack (sPlus :: prog') = sExecute st stack prog' := by
1352-  rcases stack with _ | ⟨_, _ | ⟨_, _⟩⟩ <;> trivial
1353-@[simp] theorem sExecute_minus_bad {st : State} {stack : List Nat} {prog' : List Sinstr}
1354-  (hs : stack.length < 2)  :
1355-  sExecute st stack (sMinus :: prog') = sExecute st stack prog' := by
1356-  rcases stack with _ | ⟨_, _ | ⟨_, _⟩⟩ <;> trivial
1357-@[simp] theorem sExecute_mult_bad {st : State} {stack : List Nat} {prog' : List Sinstr}
1358-  (hs : stack.length < 2)  :
1359-  sExecute st stack (sMult :: prog') = sExecute st stack prog' := by
1360-  rcases stack with _ | ⟨_, _ | ⟨_, _⟩⟩ <;> trivial
1361-
1362-example : sExecute ∅ [] [sPush 5, sPush 3, sPush 1, sMinus] = [2, 5] := by
1363-  rfl
1364-
1365-example : sExecute (X →ₜ 3) [3, 4] [sPush 4, sLoad X, sMult, sPlus] = [15, 4] := by
1366-  rfl

1368---  Next, write a function that compiles an `Aexp` into a stack machine
1369---  program. The effect of running the program should be the same as
1370---  pushing the value of the expression on the stack.
1371-
1372-def sCompile (a : Aexp) : List Sinstr :=
1373-  (match a with
1374-  | .num n        => [sPush n]
1375-  | .id x         => [sLoad x]
1376-  | .plus a₁ a₂   => sCompile a₁ ++ sCompile a₂ ++ [sPlus]
1377-  | .minus a₁ a₂  => sCompile a₁ ++ sCompile a₂ ++ [sMinus]
1378-  | .mult a₁ a₂   => sCompile a₁ ++ sCompile a₂ ++ [sMult])
1379-
1380-@[simp]
1381-theorem sCompile_num (n : Nat) : sCompile (Aexp.num n) = [sPush n] := rfl
1382-@[simp]
1383-theorem sCompile_id (x : String) : sCompile (Aexp.id x) = [sLoad x] := rfl
1384-@[simp]
1385-theorem sCompile_plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
1386-  sCompile (Aexp.plus a₁ a₂) = sCompile a₁ ++ sCompile a₂ ++ [sPlus] := rfl
1387-@[simp]
1388-theorem sCompile_minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
1389-  sCompile (Aexp.minus a₁ a₂) = sCompile a₁ ++ sCompile a₂ ++ [sMinus] := rfl
1390-@[simp]
1391-theorem sCompile_mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
1392-  sCompile (Aexp.mult a₁ a₂) = sCompile a₁ ++ sCompile a₂ ++ [sMult] := rfl
1393-

1400---  ### Exercise (3 stars): execute_app ⭐⭐⭐
1401-
1402---  Execution can be decomposed in the following sense: executing stack
1403---  program `p₁ ++ p₂` is the same as executing `p₁`, taking the resulting
1404---  stack, and executing `p₂` from that stack. Prove that fact.
1405-
1406-theorem execute_app (st : State) (p₁ p₂ : List Sinstr) (stack : List Nat) :
1407-    sExecute st stack (p₁ ++ p₂) = sExecute st (sExecute st stack p₁) p₂ := by
1408-  induction p₁ generalizing p₂ stack with
1409-  | nil => rfl
1410-  | cons a p' ih =>
1411-    cases a with
1412-    | sPush | sLoad => simp_all
1413-    | sPlus | sMinus | sMult =>
1414-      if hs : stack.length < 2 then
1415-        simp [hs, ih]
1416-      else
1417-        rcases stack with _ | ⟨_, _ | ⟨_, _⟩⟩ <;> simp_all
1418-
1419---  ### Exercise (3 stars): compiler_correct ⭐⭐⭐
1420-
1421---  Now we'll prove the correctness of the compiler implemented in the
1422---  previous exercise. Begin by proving the following lemma. If it becomes
1423---  difficult, consider whether your implementation of `sExecute` or
1424---  `sCompile` could be simplified.
1425-
1426-theorem sCompile_correct_aux (st : State) (a : Aexp) (stack : List Nat) :
1427-  sExecute st stack (sCompile a) = Aexp.eval st a :: stack := by
1428-  induction a generalizing st stack <;>
1429-  simp_all [List.append_assoc, execute_app] <;>
1430-  rfl
1431-
1432---  The main theorem should be a very easy corollary of that lemma.
1433-
1434-theorem sCompile_correct (st : State) (a : Aexp) :
1435-  sExecute st [] (sCompile a) = [ Aexp.eval st a ] := by
1436-  apply sCompile_correct_aux
1437-
1438-end StackCompiler

1440---  ### Exercise (3 stars): short_circuit (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
1441-
1442---  Most modern programming languages use a "short-circuit" evaluation rule
1443---  for boolean `and`: to evaluate `BExp.and b₁ b₂`, first evaluate `b₁`.
1444---  If it evaluates to `false`, then the entire `and` expression evaluates
1445---  to `false` immediately, without evaluating `b₂`. Otherwise, `b₂` is
1446---  evaluated to determine the result of the `and` expression.
1447-
1448---  Write an alternate version of `BExp.eval` that performs short-circuit
1449---  evaluation of `BAnd` in this manner, and prove that it is equivalent to
1450---  `BExp.eval`. (N.b. This is only true because expression evaluation in
1451---  Imp is rather simple. In a bigger language where evaluating an
1452---  expression might diverge, the short-circuiting `and` would *not* be
1453---  equivalent to the original, since it would make more programs
1454---  terminate.)
1455-
1456-def Bexp.evalSC (st : State) (b : Bexp) : Bool := (
1457-  match b with
1458-  | .bool b      =>  b
1459-  | .eq   a₁ a₂  =>  a₁.eval st == a₂.eval st
1460-  | .neq  a₁ a₂  =>  a₁.eval st != a₂.eval st
1461-  | .le   a₁ a₂  =>  decide (a₁.eval st ≤ a₂.eval st)
1462-  | .gt   a₁ a₂  =>  decide (a₁.eval st > a₂.eval st)
1463-  | .not  b₁     =>  !b₁.evalSC st
1464-  | .and  b₁ b₂  =>  match (b₁.evalSC st) with
1465-                    | false => false
1466-                    | true => b₂.evalSC st)
1467-
1468-@[simp]
1469-theorem Bexp.evalSC_bool (st : State) (b : Bool) : (Bexp.bool b).evalSC st = b := rfl
1470-@[simp]
1471-theorem Bexp.evalSC_eq (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
1472-  (Bexp.eq a₁ a₂).evalSC st = (a₁.eval st == a₂.eval st) := rfl
1473-@[simp]
1474-theorem Bexp.evalSC_neq (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
1475-  (Bexp.neq a₁ a₂).evalSC st = (a₁.eval st != a₂.eval st) := rfl
1476-@[simp]
1477-theorem Bexp.evalSC_le (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
1478-  (Bexp.le a₁ a₂).evalSC st = decide (a₁.eval st ≤  a₂.eval st) := rfl
1479-@[simp]
1480-theorem Bexp.evalSC_gt (st : State) (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) :
1481-  (Bexp.gt a₁ a₂).evalSC st = decide (a₁.eval st >  a₂.eval st) := rfl
1482-@[simp]
1483-theorem Bexp.evalSC_not (st : State) (b : Bexp) :
1484-  (Bexp.not b).evalSC st = !b.evalSC st := rfl
1485-@[simp]
1486-theorem Bexp.evalSC_and (st : State) (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) :
1487-  (Bexp.and  b₁ b₂).evalSC st = match (b₁.evalSC st) with
1488-                                | false => false
1489-                                | true => b₂.evalSC st := rfl

1496---  ### Exercise (3 stars): break_imp (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
1497-
1498---  Imperative languages like C and Java often include a `break` or similar
1499---  statement for interrupting the execution of loops. In this exercise we
1500---  consider how to add `break` to Imp. First, we need to enrich the
1501---  language of commands with an additional case. Because `break` is a
1502---  reserved keyword in Lean, we will abbreviate it as `brk`.
1503-
1504-namespace BreakImp
1505-
1506-inductive Com where
1507-  | skip
1508-  | brk                          -- <--- NEW
1509-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
1510-  | seq (c₁ c₂ : Com)
1511-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c₁ c₂ : Com)
1512-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
1513-
1514---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: commands, macro rules)
1515-
1516-namespace Com
1517-
1518-open Lean in
1519-scoped macro_rules
1520-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
1521-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
1522-    else if x.getId == `brk then `(Com.brk)
1523-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip' or 'break', got '{x.getId}'"
1524-  | `(imp { $c₁; $c₂ }) =>
1525-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c₁}) (imp {$c₂}))
1526-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
1527-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
1528-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c₁} else {$c₂} }) =>
1529-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c₁}) (imp {$c₂}))
1530-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
1531-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
1532-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
1533-    pure c
1534-
1535-end Com

1543-partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) :=
1544-  delabComInnerFor ``Com do
1545-    let e ← getExpr
1546-    guard <| e.isConstOf ``Com.brk
1547-    annAsTerm (← `(imp_com| $(mkIdent `brk):ident))
1548-

1550-  delab app.BreakImp.Com.seq, delab app.BreakImp.Com.cond, delab app.BreakImp.Com.whileDo]

1558-/--
1559-info: imp {
1560-  brk
1561-} : Com
1562--/
1563-#guard_msgs in
1564-#check imp {brk}
1565-
1566---  END DETAILS
1567-
1568---  Next, we need to define the behavior of `brk`. Informally, whenever
1569---  `brk` is executed in a sequence of commands, it stops the execution of
1570---  that sequence and signals that the innermost enclosing loop should
1571---  terminate. (If there aren't any enclosing loops, then the whole program
1572---  simply terminates.) The final state should be the same as the one in
1573---  which the `brk` statement was executed.
1574-
1575---  One important point is what to do when there are multiple loops
1576---  enclosing a given `brk`. In those cases, `brk` should only terminate
1577---  the *innermost* loop. Thus, after executing the following...
1578-
1579---        X := 0;
1580---        Y := 1;
1581---        while (0 <> Y) {
1582---          while (true) {
1583---            break
1584---          };
1585---          X := 1;
1586---          Y := Y - 1
1587---        }
1588-
1589---  ... the value of `X` should be `1`, and not `0`.
1590-
1591---  One way of expressing this behavior is to add another parameter to the
1592---  evaluation relation that specifies whether evaluation of a command
1593---  executes a `brk` statement:
1594-
1595-inductive Result : Type where
1596-  | sContinue
1597-  | sBreak
1598-
1599-open Result
1600-
1601---  We will use the syntax `st =[ c ]=> st' // s` to mean that, if `c` is
1602---  started in state `st`, then it terminates in state `st'` and either
1603---  signals that the innermost surrounding loop (or the whole program)
1604---  should exit immediately (`s = sBreak`) or that execution should
1605---  continue normally (`s = sContinue`).
1606-
1607---  The definition of the `st =[ c ]=> st' // s` relation is very similar
1608---  to the one we gave above for the regular evaluation relation
1609---  (`st =[ c ]=> st'`) -- we just need to handle the termination signals
1610---  appropriately:
1611-
1612---  - If the command is `skip`, then the state doesn't change and execution
1613---    of any enclosing loop can continue normally.
1614-
1615---  - If the command is `brk`, the state stays unchanged but we signal a
1616---    `sBreak`.
1617-
1618---  - If the command is an assignment, then we update the binding for that
1619---    variable in the state accordingly and signal that execution can
1620---    continue normally.
1621-
1622---  - If the command is of the form `if (b) {c₁} {c₂}`, then the state is
1623---    updated as in the original semantics of Imp, except that we also
1624---    propagate the signal from the execution of whichever branch was
1625---    taken.
1626-
1627---  - If the command is a sequence `c₁ ; c₂`, we first execute `c₁`. If
1628---    this yields a `sBreak`, we skip the execution of `c₂` and propagate
1629---    the `sBreak` signal to the surrounding context; the resulting state
1630---    is the same as the one obtained by executing `c₁` alone. Otherwise,
1631---    we execute `c₂` on the state obtained after executing `c₁`, and
1632---    propagate the signal generated there.
1633-
1634---  - Finally, for a loop of the form `while (b) {c}`, the semantics is
1635---    almost the same as before. The only difference is that, when `b`
1636---    evaluates to `true`, we execute `c` and check the signal that it
1637---    raises. If that signal is `sContinue`, then the execution proceeds as
1638---    in the original semantics. Otherwise, we stop the execution of the
1639---    loop, and the resulting state is the same as the one resulting from
1640---    the execution of the current iteration. In either case, since `break`
1641---    only terminates the innermost loop, `while` signals `sContinue`.
1642-
1643---  Based on the above description, complete the definition of the
1644---  `Com.EvalR` relation:
1645-
1646-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Result → Prop where
1647-  | skip {st : State} : EvalR (imp {skip}) st st sContinue
1648-  | brk {st : State}  : EvalR (imp {brk}) st st sBreak
1649-  | asgn {st : State} {a : Aexp} {n : Nat} {x : Ident} (h : a.eval st = n) :
1650-      EvalR (imp {x := ~a}) st (x →ₜ n ; st) sContinue
1651-  | seqContinue {c₁ c₂ : Com} {st st' st'' : State} {s : Result}
1652-      (h₁ : EvalR c₁ st st' sContinue)
1653-      (h₂ : EvalR c₂ st' st'' s) :
1654-      EvalR (imp {~c₁; ~c₂}) st st'' s
1655-  | seqBreak {c₁ c₂ : Com} {st st' : State} (h : EvalR c₁ st st' sBreak) :
1656-      EvalR (imp {~c₁; ~c₂}) st st' sBreak
1657-  | ifTrue {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c₁ c₂ : Com} {s : Result} (hb : b.eval st = true)
1658-      (hc : EvalR c₁ st st' s) :
1659-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}) st st' s
1660-  | ifFalse {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c₁ c₂ : Com} {s : Result} (hb : b.eval st = false)
1661-      (hc : EvalR c₂ st st' s) :
1662-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}) st st' s
1663-  | whileFalse {b : Bexp} {st : State} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false) :
1664-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st sContinue
1665-  | whileContinue {st st' st'' : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
1666-      (hc : EvalR c st st' sContinue)
1667-      (hloop : EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st' st'' sContinue) :
1668-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st'' sContinue
1669-  | whileBreak {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
1670-      (hc : EvalR c st st' sBreak) :
1671-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st' sContinue
1672-

1785---  A `for` loop should be parameterized by (a) a statement executed
1786---  initially, (b) a test that is run on each iteration of the loop to
1787---  determine whether the loop should continue, (c) a statement executed at
1788---  the end of each loop iteration, and (d) a statement that makes up the
1789---  body of the loop. (You don't need to worry about making up a concrete
1790---  Notation for `for` loops, but feel free to play with this too if you
1791---  like.)

1+module
2+
3+-- This will let the code actions spread to extracted projects
4+public import Batteries.CodeAction
5+public meta import Lean.Elab.BuiltinCommand
6+
7+namespace SLFCommand
8+
9+open Lean Elab Command
10+
11+meta section
12+
13+-- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
14+-- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
15+-- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
16+-- through spanshot tasks.
17+private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
18+  match (← get).scopes with
19+  | [] => act
20+  | h :: t =>
21+    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
22+    try
23+      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
24+      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
25+      act
26+    finally
27+      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
28+        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
29+        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
30+
31+private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
32+  let savedState ← get
33+  try
34+    m
35+  finally
36+    let state ← get
37+    set { savedState with
38+      -- Preserve the info tree
39+      infoState := state.infoState
40+      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
41+
42+namespace IndentedCommands
43+
44+/-! # Block Commands Parser
45+  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
46+  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
47+  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
48+  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
49+  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
50+  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
51+-/
52+
53+open Parser
54+
55+private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
56+  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
57+
58+/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
59+private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
60+  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
61+
62+/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
63+  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
64+  requiring the indentation.
65+-/
66+private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
67+  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
68+  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
69+    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
70+
71+private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
72+  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
73+
74+private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
75+
76+@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
77+private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
78+
79+@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
80+private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
81+
82+private partial def runRawCmdsAux
83+    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
84+  let state ← get
85+  let scope := state.scopes.head!
86+  let pctx :=  {
87+      env := state.env
88+      options := scope.opts
89+      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
90+      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
91+    }
92+  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
93+  modify fun state => { state with messages }
94+  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
95+    elabCommand cmd
96+    runLinters cmd
97+    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
98+      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
99+
100+/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
101+private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
102+  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
103+    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
104+  let fileName ← getFileName
105+  let fileMap ← getFileMap
106+  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
107+  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
108+  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
109+  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
110+  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
111+    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
112+      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
113+    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
114+  else
115+    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
116+
117+end IndentedCommands
118+
119+end
120+
121+public meta section
122+
123+open Parser IndentedCommands
124+
125+/--
126+Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
127+but discards their effects afterwards.
128+
129+Example:
130+```lean
131+sf_experiment
132+  def hidden : Nat := 1
133+  #check hidden
134+-- `hidden` is not available here.
135+```
136+-/
137+def experimentTk := leading_parser
138+  "sf_experiment"
139+
140+@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
141+  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
142+    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
143+
144+/--
145+Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
146+Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
147+
148+Example:
149+```lean
150+sf_expect_failure
151+  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
152+```
153+-/
154+def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
155+  "sf_expect_failure"
156+
157+/-
158+  Like `sf_expect_failure` but reports the diagnostics.
159+-/
160+def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
161+  "sf_expect_failure?"
162+
163+@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
164+  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
165+    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
166+
167+@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
168+  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
169+    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
170+
171+@[command_elab experimentCmd]
172+def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
173+  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
174+  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
175+    runRawCmds body
176+
177+@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
178+def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
179+  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
180+  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
181+    throwUnsupportedSyntax
182+  let tk := stx[0]
183+  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
184+  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
185+    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
186+
187+end
188+
189+namespace Tests
190+
191+/--
192+@ +3:11...+4:8
193+info: unexpected token '#check'; expected 'with'
194+---
195+@ +3:4...9
196+info: Missing cases:
197+_
198+---
199+@ +4:2...8
200+info: 1 : Nat
201+-/
202+#guard_msgs (positions := true) in
203+sf_expect_failure?
204+  def f (n : Nat) : Nat :=
205+    match n
206+  #check 1
207+
208+/-- info: Nat : Type -/
209+#guard_msgs in
210+#check Nat
211+
212+/--
213+info: SLFCommand.Tests.x : Nat
214+---
215+info: 3
216+-/
217+#guard_msgs in
218+sf_experiment
219+  def x : Nat := 1
220+  #check x
221+  def f : Nat → Nat
222+    | 0 => 0
223+    | n + 1 => n + 2
224+  #eval f 2
225+
226+/-- error: Unknown identifier `x` -/
227+#guard_msgs in
228+#check x
229+
230+/--
231+error: Type mismatch
232+  "qwq"
233+has type
234+  String
235+but is expected to have type
236+  Nat
237+-/
238+#guard_msgs in
239+sf_experiment
240+  def y : Nat := "qwq"
241+
242+/-- info: invalid 'import' command, it must be used in the beginning of the file -/
243+#guard_msgs in
244+sf_expect_failure?
245+  import Lean
246+
247+/-- warning: using 'exit' to interrupt Lean -/
248+#guard_msgs in
249+sf_experiment
250+  #exit
251+
252+end Tests
253+
254+end SLFCommand

357---  ### Inference Rule Notation
358-
359---  In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
360---  `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form
361---  of *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the
362---  conclusion below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be
363---  written like this as an inference rule:
364-
365---  a₁ ⇓ n₁
366---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
367---                      ------------------          (plus)
368---                      plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂

371---  of the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
372-
373---  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
374---          EvalR a₁ n₁ →
375---          EvalR a₂ n₂ →
376---          EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
377-
378---  Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
379---  informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the
380---  right as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks
381---  between the premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as
382---  `→`. All the variables mentioned in the rule (`a₁`, `n₁`, etc.) are
383---  implicitly bound by universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such
384---  variables are often called *metavariables* to distinguish them from the
385---  variables of whatever language we are defining. At the moment, our
386---  arithmetic expressions don't include variables, but we'll soon be
387---  adding them.) The whole collection of rules is understood as being
388---  wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In informal prose,
389---  this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let `Aexp.EvalR`

357+-- ### Inference Rule Notation
358+
359+-- In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
360+-- `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form of
361+-- *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the conclusion
362+-- below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be written like
363+-- this as an inference rule:
364+
365+-- a₁ ⇓ n₁
366+--                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
367+--                     ------------------          (plus)
368+--                     plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
369+
370+-- Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version of
371+-- the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
372+
373+-- | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
374+--         EvalR a₁ n₁ →
375+--         EvalR a₂ n₂ →
376+--         EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
377+
378+-- Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
379+-- informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the right
380+-- as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks between the
381+-- premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as `→`. All the
382+-- variables mentioned in the rule (`a₁`, `n₁`, etc.) are implicitly bound by
383+-- universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such variables are often called
384+-- *metavariables* to distinguish them from the variables of whatever language
385+-- we are defining. At the moment, our arithmetic expressions don't include
386+-- variables, but we'll soon be adding them.) The whole collection of rules is
387+-- understood as being wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In
388+-- informal prose, this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let
389+-- `Aexp.EvalR` be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
390+
391+-- To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single inductive
392+-- definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor name; above the
393+-- line are the premises, below the line the conclusion; metavariables like
394+-- `a₁` and `n₁` are implicitly universally quantified. The whole collection
395+-- of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation closed under them:
396+
397+-- ---------                (num)
398+--                         num n ⇓ n

648---  At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use
649---  by default?
650-
651---  Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
652---  definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable,
653---  relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand,
654---  and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles from them.
655---  On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
656---  deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove*
657---  these if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to
658---  simplify them during proofs.
659-
660---  In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both*
661---  styles plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to
662---  switch between points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
663---  `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.
664-

651+-- default?

653+-- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
654+-- definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable, relational
655+-- definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand, and Lean
656+-- generates useful inversion and induction principles from them. On the other
657+-- hand, functional definitions are automatically deterministic and total --
658+-- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these if we need them -- and we
659+-- can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify them during proofs.
660+
661+-- In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both* styles
662+-- plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to switch between
663+-- points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
664+-- `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.
665+

302-sf_recall_source
303-  /--
304-    `BEq α` is a typeclass for supplying a boolean-valued equality relation on
305-    `α`, notated as `a == b`. Unlike `DecidableEq α` (which uses `a = b`), this
306-    is `Bool` valued instead of `Prop` valued, and it also does not have any
307-    axioms like being reflexive or agreeing with `=`. It is mainly intended for
308-    programming applications. See `LawfulBEq` for a version that requires that
309-    `==` and `=` coincide.
310-  
311-    Typically we prefer to put the "more variable" term on the left,
312-    and the "more constant" term on the right.
313-    -/
314-    class BEq (α : Type u) where
315-      /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/

408---  This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to
409---  define mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about
410---  how those operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a
411---  typeclass to define a *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that
412---  includes four things:
413-
414---  - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
415-
416---  - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
417---    elements of type `α` into one,
418-
419---  - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
420---    element", and
421-
422---  - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
423-
424---    - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
425-
426---    - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is
427---      associative)
428-
429---  We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
385+-- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to define
386+-- mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about how those
387+-- operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a
388+-- *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
389+
390+-- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
391+
392+-- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
393+--   elements of type `α` into one,
394+
395+-- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
396+--   element", and
397+
398+-- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
399+
400+--   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
401+--   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is associative)
402+
403+-- We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
430404 
431405 -- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
432406 class OpSet (α : Type) where
440414   right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
441415   assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
442416

446---  `OpSet`, similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.

490---  In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
491---  properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on
492---  the typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity
493---  element of a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the
494---  same set with the same operator, their identity elements must also be
495---  the same:
459+-- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
460+-- properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on the
461+-- typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity element of
462+-- a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set with
463+-- the same operator, their identity elements must also be the same:

497465 theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
498466   obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
507475   -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
508476   exact h'
509477

519---  arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal
520---  as `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.

526493 class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where

529496   right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id
530497

537+-- ## Maps
538+
539+-- *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in ordinary
540+-- programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're going to need
541+-- them in many places in later volumes.
542+
543+-- We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a "default"
544+-- element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't exist, and
545+-- *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate success or
546+-- failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as
547+-- the default element.
548+
549+-- ### Key and Value Types
550+
551+-- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to index
552+-- into our maps and a type for the values the maps return. In this section,
553+-- we'll use the type variable `α` for the type of keys and `β` for values. In
554+-- addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, our key type `α` requires
555+-- instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq` typeclasses:
556+
557+-- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
558+-- class ReflBEq (α : Type) [BEq α] : Prop where
559+--   /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
560+--   protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
561+
562+-- /--
563+-- A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
564+
565+-- In other words:
566+--  * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
567+--  * `a == a` is true.
568+-- -/
569+-- class LawfulBEq (α : Type) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
570+--   /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
571+--   eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
572+
573+-- These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is reflexive and
574+-- coincides with proposition equality `=`.
575+
576+-- In general, we place no constraints on the value type `β`.
577+
578+-- ### Total Maps
579+
580+-- The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`, with
581+-- a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs. Here, we
582+-- are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead. The advantage
583+-- of this representation is that it offers a more *extensional* view of maps,
584+-- as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two maps that respond to
585+-- every query in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
586+-- function, rather than just as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies
587+-- proofs that use maps.
588+
589+-- Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them inside a
590+-- `structure` which we call `TotalMap`. Intuitively, a total map just
591+-- contains a function `inner` from a key of type `α` to a value of type `β`.
630592 
631593 structure TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
632594   inner : α → β
633595 
634596 namespace TotalMap
635597 
636---  In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
637---  typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our
638---  `DefaultValue` example from above:
639-
640---  The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a
641---  default element; this map always returns the default element when
642---  applied to any key.
598+-- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
599+-- typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our
600+-- `DefaultValue` example from above:
601+
602+-- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a default
603+-- element; this map always returns the default element when applied to any
604+-- key.
643605 
644606 def empty {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : TotalMap α β where
645607   inner := fun _ ↦ default
646608 
647---  These types and implicit instances are now available automatically to
648---  all the definitions in this section.
649-
650---  Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above hooked `==` and
651---  `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can declare an instance of the
652---  standard library's `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with
653---  this empty map.
609+-- These types and implicit instances are now available automatically to all
610+-- the definitions in this section.
611+
612+-- Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above hooked `==` and
613+-- `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can declare an instance of the
614+-- standard library's `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with this
615+-- empty map.
654616 
655617 instance {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
656618   emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
657619 
658620 theorem empty_def {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : (∅ : TotalMap α β) = { inner := fun _ ↦ default } := by rfl
659621

665---  #### Getting Elements
666-
667---  While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions under the hood,
668---  we would prefer not to expose this fact in its public interface.
669---  Accordingly, we define new operations for querying and updating
670---  mappings. We define a function `get` for getting the value associated
671---  with a key playing the role that `find` played for the Lists chapter's
672---  list-based maps,
626+-- #### Getting Elements
627+
628+-- While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions under the hood, we
629+-- would prefer not to expose this fact in its public interface. Accordingly,
630+-- we define new operations for querying and updating mappings. We define a
631+-- function `get` for getting the value associated with a key playing the role
632+-- that `find` played for the Lists chapter's list-based maps,
673633 
674634 def get {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) := m.inner a
675635 
679639 
680640 example : emptyNatMap.get 2 = 0 := by rfl
681641 
682---  Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def` and `get_def`:
642+-- Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def` and `get_def`:
683643 
684644 example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = 0 := by
685645   rewrite [get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
686646   rfl
687647 
688---  In the above example, we use `rewrite` and `rfl` instead of the usual

1329+-- booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).

1331+-- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1332+
1333+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1334+--     Check formatting:

1336+-- - ⠀

1349+-- The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1350+-- (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1351+-- number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1352+-- mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1353+
1354+-- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only by
1355+-- functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false` in
1356+-- finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1357+-- argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1358+-- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1359+
1360+-- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1361+-- mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1362+-- contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1363+-- halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this essential
1364+-- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we
1365+-- need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this
1366+-- only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1367+
1368+-- The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1369+-- functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly to
1370+-- justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1371+-- required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1372+-- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property that
1373+-- happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation
1374+-- or as a function into Prop.
1375+

1-module
2-
3-public meta import Lean.Elab.BuiltinCommand
4-
5-namespace SFLCompat.Experiment
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-
9-meta section
10-
11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39-
40-namespace IndentedCommands
41-
42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure_in`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure_in` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end
118-
119-public meta section
120-
121-open Parser IndentedCommands
122-
123-/--
124-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125-but discards their effects afterwards.
126-
127-Example:
128-```lean
129-sf_experiment
130-  def hidden : Nat := 1
131-  #check hidden
132--- `hidden` is not available here.
133-```
134--/
135-def experimentTk := leading_parser
136-  "sf_experiment"
137-
138-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141-
142-/--
143-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145-
146-Example:
147-```lean
148-sf_expect_failure_in
149-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150-```
151--/
152-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153-  "sf_expect_failure_in"
154-
155-/-
156-  Like `sf_expect_failure_in` but reports the diagnostics.
157--/
158-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159-  "sf_expect_failure_in?"
160-
161-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164-
165-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168-
169-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173-    runRawCmds body
174-
175-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180-  let tk := stx[0]
181-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184-
185-end
